gaps.title: Nothing marks an invoice overdue
gaps.testCoverage: tests/overdue-invoices.test.ts (8), scripts/verify-overdue-invoices.mjs (11 live checks)
gaps.evidence: finance.mark_overdue_invoices runs on the cron tick and performs the transition INVOICE_TRANSITIONS has admitted since the first day: issued and partially_paid become overdue once due_at has passed. Not a new rule - an existing one executed for the first time. It takes each row for update skip locked, restates the status on the write so a payment landing in the same instant wins, and audits only what it actually changed. It chases nobody: a payment reminder is client-facing and waits on the outbound policy rather than arriving behind a status change. Five statuses are deliberately untouched - draft, pending_approval, paid, void, and anything with no due date.

gaps.title: Refunds unimplemented
gaps.testCoverage: tests/refunds.test.ts (11), scripts/verify-refunds.mjs (14 live checks)
gaps.evidence: finance.refunds records money going back as its own row, because finance/schema.ts has said since the first day that paid is terminal and money returned is a refund rather than a status flip. Three rules, none invented here: a refund needs an approved approval behind it (directive 28 RED, 29 the Admin's; the engine already carried 'refund' as a subject type and its money floor already refused any policy naming below owner); it cannot exceed what came in, computed under the invoice lock and refused rather than clamped, counting requests still waiting so two owners cannot approve the same balance; and the invoice is untouched. Recording is idempotent on the provider reference, re-checks the ceiling because an approval from yesterday must still fit today, and both the asking and the leaving are audited. The invoice screen now drives it: refunds are listed with their state, an owner may ask for one against the available balance, and recording that the money left is a separate control - one control doing both would be a refund with no approval behind it. Neither the form nor the action inspects the approval; the database refuses an unapproved recording and a copy of that rule in TypeScript could drift.

gaps.title: Payment status vocabulary mismatch
gaps.testCoverage: tests/payment-verified.test.ts (31), scripts/verify-milestone-invoicing.mjs section 7f rewritten to prove the new rule against real Postgres: a fully recorded invoice stays unpaid and publishes no invoice.paid until somebody confirms.
gaps.evidence: Closed with G-007. The vocabulary question this gap asked - what the payment states mean - is answered by the two numbers rather than by renaming statuses: a payment is recorded (status captured, verified_at null) or confirmed (verified_at set, verified_by named). The provider-side status machine created/authorized/captured/failed/refunded is untouched, because it describes what a provider said; verification describes what the agency believes, and conflating them is what made a client's claim sufficient to advance delivery.

gaps.title: Payment verified has no distinct meaning
gaps.testCoverage: tests/payment-verified.test.ts (31), scripts/verify-milestone-invoicing.mjs section 7f rewritten to prove the new rule against real Postgres: a fully recorded invoice stays unpaid and publishes no invoice.paid until somebody confirms.
gaps.evidence: Closed under ADM-04. Recording money and believing it are two acts now. finance.payments carries verified_at and verified_by; finance.invoices carries verified_minor beside paid_minor. paid_minor keeps its exact meaning, so invoices_paid_not_over_total, the overpayment refusal and the refund ceiling are all untouched - what may not exceed the invoice is what has been claimed, and verification only decides what has been believed. status = paid and the invoice.paid event follow verified_minor, which means the event that opens the next milestone is now published by somebody who looked at a bank statement rather than by whoever typed in what a client said. record_manual_payment was carried forward from its own latest definition with three marked edits rather than regenerated, because regenerating replace_payment_plan from the wrong migration is exactly how D16 was silently reverted. Existing rows are backfilled as verified: they were recorded when recording was confirming, and marking them unverified would un-pay every invoice in the system to claim a distinction nobody was offered at the time.

gaps.title: the six sales activities ADM-10 names cannot be recorded
gaps.testCoverage: tests/sales-activities.test.ts (13); tests/workflow-regression.test.ts still pins the stage set
gaps.implementationState: both halves satisfied. The stage half always was - four stages plus the off-ramp. The activity half is now built: the six kinds ADM-10 section 7 names are in the lead_activities CHECK, recordSalesActivity writes them, and the audit log records each as what it is rather than as a note.
gaps.productionVerificationState: not verified in production - no real lead has had one of the six recorded against a production database
gaps.evidence: AUDIT 2026-08-14, against granted ADM-10 as written at docs/business-os/02-business-rules.md section 7. STAGE HALF - SATISFIED EXACTLY. Section 7: "The pipeline stays four stages: discovery -> proposal -> negotiation -> won, with lost off any of them." The four stages are the four; `lost` is the off-ramp section 7 describes, not a fifth stage. OPPORTUNITY_STAGES carries ['discovery','proposal','negotiation','won','lost'] and the sales.opportunities CHECK carries the same five values, which is four stages plus the off-ramp. The earlier suspicion that 'four stages' might conflict with a five-value enum is resolved: section 7 spells the four out by name and names `lost` separately. ACTIVITY HALF - NOT SATISFIED. Section 7 requires that contacted, sample sent, demo sent, offer sent, follow-up and advance requested be recorded as timestamped activities on the lead. crm.lead_activities.kind is CHECK-constrained to ('note','status_change','message_in','message_out','call','agent_run','assignment') - none of the six. Searched the whole tree: sample_sent, demo_sent, offer_sent and advance_requested appear NOWHERE in src/, supabase/, app/ or tests/. The only matches for the other two are unrelated - 'contacted' is prose in a finance comment, and follow_up is crm.leads.next_follow_up_at, a date column that nothing reads (G-012). So the six states the decision moved OUT of the pipeline were never given the home it moved them to. NOT A BLOCKER, and one open design question that is not a business decision: whether the six become new `kind` values or ride an existing kind with metadata, the shape G-016 used for `returning`. ADM-10 names the six, so the vocabulary is specified either way. NOT CHANGED by this audit, per instruction: the enum, the transitions, the CHECK constraint and the data are all untouched. CLOSED 2026-08-14. Six kinds added to the CHECK, exactly the six section 7 names and no more, with a test asserting each appears in the business-rules document itself so an invented seventh fails. recordSalesActivity follows addLeadNote rather than setLeadStatus, because these are things that happened rather than transitions, and nothing is validated against the deal stage - section 7 is explicit that the two are independent. AUDIT VOCABULARY: the six are audited as lead.contacted, lead.sample_sent, lead.demo_sent, lead.offer_sent, lead.follow_up_recorded and lead.advance_requested. The seven older kinds keep lead.note_added, which is wrong for an assignment and is deliberately NOT fixed here - changing it alters what the audit log says about behaviour nobody is touching. Raised separately as G-126. Six new kinds filed as notes would have been six new false statements written knowingly into the audit log, in the change that exists to make the six honest. NEAR MISS WORTH RECORDING: the first draft regenerated audit.record_row_change from 20260813120013 while the live definition is the later 20260813120019. A diff before trusting it showed the regeneration would have flipped security invoker to definer, changed new.qualification to new.qualified_at, swapped the audit insert for core.record_audit, and DROPPED THE proposals BRANCH ENTIRELY - which would have made every proposal write raise "no vocabulary for table". The function was rebuilt programmatically from the live text with one branch substituted, and a test now pins four markers of the live definition so a future regeneration fails in CI.

gaps.title: Proposals have tables but no code
gaps.testCoverage: tests/quotations.test.ts (40), scripts/verify-quotations.mjs (50 live)
gaps.evidence: Built. sales.proposals and proposal_items had tables, RLS and a version column from day one and no code at all. ADM-07 - staff draft, the owner approves, then it is sent - is now held in Postgres: the version is allocated under the opportunity's lock, the subtotal is summed from the lines and the line's own amount is derived from its quantity and price (a caller-supplied total would choose its own approver, because submit_proposal hands the total to the policy ladder), a version is frozen the moment it leaves draft in both its terms and its lines, sending refuses anything the owner has not approved, and a client's answer is only taken from `sent` - Document 09 section 18's "do not mark accepted simply because quote was delivered". Only one version is live per deal (section 16), enforced by a partial unique index rather than intended; drafting the next one supersedes the previous and cancels the approval it was waiting on. approval_policies_money_floor gains 'proposal' so no policy may name below the owner, which is what ADM-07 said and what proposal.approve has always meant. Acceptance deliberately does not win the deal - section 22 puts payment in between.

gaps.title: Follow-up automation
gaps.testCoverage: tests/follow-up-rhythms (25), follow-up-contract (28), sent-is-terminal (5); scripts/verify-follow-up-sequences (27), verify-follow-up-worker (54), verify-follow-up-delivery (38). RED PROOFS, each shown to fail: attempt uniqueness dropped -> 2 attempts; revalidation removed -> 5 failures; escalate guard removed -> both callers true; pending-only settle guard restored -> retry truthfulness fails; jobs dedupe index dropped -> a crashed-dispatcher replay enqueues a second job. One check was found DECORATIVE by red proof - the second-dispatch check was guarded by published_at, not the dedupe key - and was rewritten to simulate the crash window the key actually protects.
gaps.status: CLOSED - every closure criterion carries execution evidence; G-137, G-138 and G-139 remain separate open blockers
gaps.blocker: none - the remaining constraints are their own gaps: G-137 (no timezone value, so nothing sends in production), G-138 (situations 2 and 3), G-139 (post-project channel)
gaps.implementationState: closed. Seven layers, each executed: ADM-69 arithmetic; the eight situations and the ten-step contract; persistence whose constraints make idempotency structural; the observer; the worker on the existing cron tick; delivery through followup.queued -> dispatcher -> core.jobs -> crm:deliverFollowUp -> the provider boundary; and the audit lifecycle. The message body is a single neutral placeholder sentence, named as one - the agent that writes real text is Phase 5 - and NOTHING can reach a client in production until an owner supplies the G-137 timezone, so no placeholder prose can either.
gaps.productionVerificationState: verified against local Postgres and CI, not production. 92 live checks across worker (54) and delivery (38) scripts, all executing real functions against real rows. The provider is substituted ONLY at the HTTP boundary via WHATSAPP_GRAPH_BASE_URL - what a stub cannot prove (Meta accepting, delivering, webhooks) remains EXTERNAL VERIFICATION REQUIRED. The delivery guarantee, worded exactly: at-most-one logical AgencyOS send per (sequence, attempt), enforced by unique constraint and derived external_ref; external provider delivery semantics remain provider-dependent, and the double-submission window after a crash-between-accept-and-record was MEASURED (the provider is hit again) rather than hidden.
gaps.evidence: crm.leads.next_follow_up_at exists, is indexed, is set by hand, and nothing reads it. ADM-11 answers whether follow-ups are auto-sent without human review - it accepts that risk explicitly - but it does not say which situations trigger one or with what timing, which the gap record has always noted. Separately and more seriously, there is NO communication permission model anywhere: crm.contacts has no opt-in, opt-out, consent or unsubscribe column, and no migration handles consent. Sending automated messages to contacts with no recorded consent is a different and larger exposure than the one ADM-11 accepted, and inventing a consent model - what it means, how it is captured, whether Meta own WhatsApp opt-in rules satisfy it - would be inventing a business decision. STEP 1 TRACING DONE 2026-08-15, and TWO VALUES WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG IF INFERRED. (1) Situation 6, pending payment, uses a FIFTH rhythm ADM-69 names Payment-Followup, states NO day values for, and marks automated DEFERRED. Reading the four rhythms and assuming payment shared one would have invented a cadence for money. It is represented with rhythm null and is unrunnable by construction. (2) Situation 5, pending approval, is recorded verbatim as INTERNAL communication, explicitly NOT governed by the client/lead consent gate - applying the consent rule there would have stopped the owner being told what needs deciding, which is G-110. THE FULL MAPPING: 1 quotation and 2 requirements-request and 3 proposal all use Sales-Active; 4 abandoned conversation and 7 inactive lead use Sales-Nurture; 5 pending approval uses Internal-Approval; 8 post-project uses Customer-Success; 6 pending payment is deferred. THE CONTRACT ORDER IS PRESERVED RATHER THAN OPTIMISED: the checks could run in any order and reach the same yes, but not the same EXPLANATION - a lead that both converted and lacks consent must be reported as converted, because that is the fact somebody acting on the report needs. PERSISTENCE ADDED 2026-08-15. THE GUARANTEE IS A CONSTRAINT, NOT CAUTION: no-duplicate-client-messages cannot be kept by a well-written handler, because two workers claiming the same row a second apart both compute the same attempt number and both believe they are first. unique (sequence_id, attempt) makes the INSERT the claim, so the loser fails on a constraint rather than on a comparison it lost. Proved with two genuinely concurrent inserts rather than sequentially. unique (organization_id, situation_key, subject_type, subject_id) stops two observations of one fact starting two sequences. subject_id deliberately carries NO foreign key: the eight situations point at four tables, seven nullable columns would grow one per situation forever, and the handler must re-read the subject before every send anyway under ADM-69 step 6. A TENANCY LINK RLS CANNOT EXPRESS: both rows carry organization_id and RLS checks each against the caller, neither against the other, so a trigger refuses a send whose organization differs from its sequence. A NEAR MISS WORTH RECORDING: that check first passed with the trigger DROPPED, because the fixture second organization used a slug containing underscores which the slug CHECK refuses, so the send carried organization_id undefined and was refused for having no organization at all. A green earned for the wrong reason, caught only by proving red. WORKER ADDED 2026-08-15 on the EXISTING cron tick, beside the approval-expiry and quotation-lapse sweeps - no second queue, because ADM-69 work is the same shape as theirs and a parallel subsystem would be a second set of retry, tenancy and idempotency rules to keep in step. ARCHITECTURE SECTION 3.2 CAUGHT THE FIRST PLACEMENT: the worker was written in src/lib/crm and lib must not depend on modules, which it does for the situation registry and the contract. Moved to src/modules/crm - the sweeps it sits beside in the tick are lib primitives that need no policy, and this is policy. TIMEZONE, G-137: core.organizations.timezone was added with an IANA-shaped CHECK and left NULL BY DESIGN. Adding storage is technical completion of a requirement ADM-69 already records; choosing the VALUE would be inventing a real-world fact. On a deployment with no zone every sequence is blocked with timezone_unavailable and NOTHING IS SENT. A BLOCK IS NOT AN ATTEMPT: a sequence blocked each minute would otherwise exhaust ADM-69 seven attempts in seven minutes and escalate about a client who ignored seven messages that were never sent. ESCALATION EXACTLY ONCE is a conditional UPDATE whose predicate includes the state it leaves, so a second worker matches no row; it returns whether THIS caller escalated, so only the winner acts. THE SEND external_ref is derived as followup:sequence:attempt rather than random, so a crash between claim and send finds the existing message instead of writing a second. EXECUTED 2026-08-15, AND EXECUTION FOUND A REAL BUG NOTHING ELSE COULD. Running the worker twice sent a SECOND message: ADM-69 states the schedule as absolute day numbers from day 0, which is unambiguous while the scheduler keeps up and says nothing about one that is late. A sequence triggered forty days ago has EVERY attempt overdue at once, so a worker running each minute sent seven messages in seven minutes - precisely what spacing 7 business days exists to prevent. Fixed by ALSO enforcing the spacing between ACTUAL SENDS: next due is the absolute schedule floored at the interval ADM-69 already records, applied from the message that was really sent. That narrows behaviour and invents nothing, and only ever makes a follow-up later. Found by running the worker twice against a real database rather than by reading the decision. A SECOND REAL DEFECT, found by tracing the lifecycle Part 2 asked for: crm.send_outbound_message writes a message as delivery pending and returns the recipient - the CALLER then calls the provider and marks delivery, which is what the announcer does inside a job handler so retry comes from the job runner. THE FOLLOW-UP WORKER CALLED send_outbound_message AND STOPPED, so every follow-up would have sat pending forever while the worker counters reported it sent. Fixed through the EXISTING path rather than a new one: the worker emits followup.queued, the catalog routes it to crm:deliverFollowUp, the dispatcher enqueues keyed on the event, and the job runner drains it through the same generic loop as the announcements - inheriting the retry budget, backoff and parking. THE HANDLER RECOMPUTES THE RECIPIENT by calling send_outbound_message again with the SAME external_ref, which answers already_sent and returns the recipient as it is now; carrying a phone number in the payload would deliver to whatever was true when the attempt was claimed. CONSENT HOLDS AT THE LAST MOMENT TOO: if it was withdrawn between claim and delivery the handler succeeds as suppressed rather than sending. ALSO FIXED: the worker script drives the REAL worker, which starts sequences for seed rows it did not create; leaving them behind made the next script observer return nothing, so it now undoes what the worker did rather than only its own fixtures. CLOSED 2026-08-15 after the delivery pass. THREE MORE DEFECTS FOUND BY EXECUTION: (1) crm.mark_outbound_delivery settled only pending messages, so a transient failure whose retry succeeded read FAILED FOREVER - in the transcript and on the operations screen, and the announcer has retried through the same window since G-110. Sent is now terminal and nothing else is: pending->sent, pending->failed and failed->sent are legal, sent->anything is refused, so the late-duplicate protection the old guard existed for survives. (2) A pending_approval reminder sequence stopped as no_conversation on its first due date - the observer deliberately selects no conversation for internal situations and the worker never resolved the internal group, so ADM-69 Internal-Approval rhythm never ran at all. The worker now resolves the internal group exactly as the announcer does. (3) The second-dispatch dedupe check was decorative - see testCoverage. SITUATIONS: 1 and 4 driven observer->worker->dispatcher->claim->handler->provider with correct rhythm, recipient, organization and thread; 5 delivers reminders to the internal group with no consent record anywhere and stops on decision; 7 was the original e2e path; 8 stops honestly under G-139; 2/3 never scheduled under G-138; payment never scheduled, DEFERRED. CONSENT: worker pre-check and chokepoint proven separately; withdrawal between claim and delivery is suppressed at the chokepoint with ZERO provider calls. AUDIT: followup.sequence_started / attempt_claimed x7 / sequence_escalated exactly once, each carrying its own organization, with per-tick bookkeeping deliberately excluded from the log. ADVERSARIAL REVIEW BEFORE MERGE, seven confirmed findings, all fixed in the same change: (1) HIGH - internalGroupFor dropped the announcer error branch, so one transient read blip permanently stopped an approval reminder sequence as no_conversation, and an absent group did the same - an organization linking its group tomorrow would never get reminders for approvals pending today. Now: read-failed blocks and retries, absent group blocks as no_internal_group and retries, and destination resolution happens BEFORE the claim so neither spends an attempt; the block-not-stop branch is exercised end to end. (2) MEDIUM - the first sent-is-terminal predicate, is distinct from sent, was WIDER than the stated rule: it admitted rows with no delivery key, which is every inbound message, so a wrong id from a service-role caller would stamp outbound state and an outbound audit row onto a client own words. Now in (pending, failed) - the stated rule exactly - and the wrong-id no-op invariant is proved against a real inbound row. (3) failed-to-sent kept the stale error key, reading as delivered and failed at once; sent now strips it. (4) the old pending-only comment survived inside the rewritten function, contradicting the predicate below it; removed. (5) the attempt-claim audit check counted globally with a dead subject_id filter - any other test leftovers could satisfy it; now scoped to this sequence send-row ids and exact. (6) the delivery script cleanup deleted outbox events and jobs globally and leaked the approval_requests row on any throw; now org-scoped with the approval owned by cleanup. (7) a duplicated conjunct asserting the same predicate twice; the lost assertion - the failure detail names the provider - restored.

gaps.title: No outbound communication channel
gaps.testCoverage: tests/outbound-messages.test.ts (16), scripts/verify-outbound-messages.mjs (16 live checks)
gaps.evidence: Built under ADM-09, taken by delegation: the inbound webhook already speaks WhatsApp Cloud API, so outbound over the same Graph API adds no vendor. crm.send_outbound_message records the message BEFORE the provider is called - a message sent and not recorded is invisible, a message recorded and not sent is visibly wrong - allocating seq under the conversation's lock and deduplicating on the caller's idempotency key. What the provider says is written back by crm.mark_outbound_delivery, which audits from inside its own transaction and refuses to re-settle a message. gaps.title: Duplicate suppression for returning clients
gaps.testCoverage: tests/returning-client.test.ts (13), scripts/verify-returning-client.mjs (16 live)
gaps.evidence: Closed, and two thirds of it already worked - measured before anything was written rather than assumed. NOTHING IN AGENCYOS DEFINES LIFETIME VALUE: lifetime, LTV, retention and churn appear in no business document, and the only occurrence anywhere is this gap own title. gaps.title: the deal pre-check has no stage filter, so a settled deal blocks a new one
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/verify-second-engagement.mjs (13 live), tests/one-deal-per-lead.test.ts (24, two of which fail against the old pre-check)
gaps.productionVerificationState: verified against a real Postgres in CI (13 live checks across seven cases) and by unit tests that fail against the previous behaviour; not exercised against production data
gaps.evidence: Fixed. ADM-05 and ADM-42: one lead per person forever, and a returning client gets a new deal on their existing lead. opportunities_open_lead_key has been partial on unsettled stages since D21, so the DATABASE has permitted a second engagement all along - createOpportunity did not. Its pre-check read any deal for the lead with no stage filter and no ordering, so a click on a lead whose only deal was lost handed that lost deal straight back, and the second engagement could never be opened from the application. Measured before the fix: the database accepted a second deal on a lost lead while the pre-check answered with "First deal (lost)". Both reads now filter by the same predicate as the index - the pre-check and the re-read that follows a 23505 on that index, the latter because the index it violated is the OPEN one, so a read without the filter could answer with an unrelated settled deal. Ordered as well as filtered: limit 1 over an unfiltered set was an unordered pick, the D22 shape. The predicate is defined once as SETTLED_OPPORTUNITY_STAGES and mirrored from the index rather than restated at each call site, which is the arrangement LIVE_PROPOSAL_STATUSES has with proposals_live_version_key. A test asserts the constant and the index agree, so the two cannot drift into answering "does this lead have a deal?" differently. Seven cases proved live: an open deal still blocks, a won one does not, a lost one does not, a reopened one blocks again because it is open once more, a new lead opens its first, concurrent attempts produce one deal not two, and a repeat request answers with the open deal rather than the settled one. Two unit tests fail against the unfixed pre-check and pass against the fix.

gaps.evidence: Closed under ADM-13, shape B of the decision document: approval PERMITS issuing rather than releasing the payment. projects.milestones.requires_deliverable_id names the deliverable whose client approval unblocks the bill, and finance.issue_invoice refuses with deliverable_not_approved while it is anything but approved - read under the same invoice lock as every other refusal, so an approval landing between a caller's check and the write cannot be missed. Drafting stays free; issuing is the act that reaches the client and is the one that waits, which is the shape the QA gate already uses when it refuses submit_deliverable rather than every write. Shape C, where approval releases the payment automatically, was argued against in the document and declined by the Admin: every other money path in this system requires a person, and the first exception should be chosen rather than arrived at. The comparison is `is distinct from 'approved'` rather than `<>`, because a deliverable row that has vanished leaves the status null and null <> 'approved' is null, which would let it through. What this does not guarantee, stated rather than discovered: a milestone with no linked deliverable issues exactly as before, so the guarantee is only as good as the linking somebody remembers to do. The alternative was inventing which deliverable gates which milestone for every project that already exists, and being wrong about some of them silently.

gaps.evidence: G-104's section 7 required a change-log row for every merge including the newest. The convention it exists to enforce is that a pull request cannot record its own merge approval - the change after it writes the row - so there is always exactly one merge outstanding, and the check did not say so. The first thing it did after merging was turn main red for PR #65, itself. A red main between every merge and the next change is how a team learns to merge past a red check, which is the same failure as an alert nobody reads. Only the newest merge is exempt now, and the pass line names it rather than staying quiet: 'with #65 outstanding for the next change to record'. One more merge and the previous number is no longer newest, so at most one may be outstanding - the convention written as an invariant. The twenty-three unlogged merges that raised G-104 would still fail here, twenty-two times.

gaps.title: a quotation past its validity date has no state of its own
gaps.testCoverage: tests/quotations.test.ts (updated, plus 3 new cases) and scripts/verify-quotations.mjs section 10b (8 live checks)
gaps.evidence: Document 09 section 15 asks a quote to carry a validity period and says nothing about what happens when it passes. G-011 enforces the one reading that is unambiguous - record_proposal_response refuses an acceptance after the date, and still accepts a refusal, because that is what a validity period means. What it does not do is move the row: a lapsed quotation still reads `sent`, so a queue of outstanding quotes counts it as live and nothing tells anybody it went cold. Whether it should expire on a timer (the shape approval expiry already uses, G-096) or simply be reported as lapsed is ADM-71. Deliberately not invented: a cron job that silently retires a client's open offer is a business decision, not an implementation detail. DECIDED 2026-08-14: ADM-71 GRANTED, option A. CONSUMER REVIEW under requirement 7, performed before any implementation, found six consumers of the sent status. Unaffected: send_proposal (approved -> sent); payment, which is tied to an accepted quote; project creation, which is separately ADM-72. DERIVABLE, recorded rather than raised: proposals_live_version_key defines live as a version "still on its way to an answer" - a lapsed quote is not, so it leaves the live set and frees the deal for a new quotation without superseding anything. That follows from the index's own stated rationale rather than from a new decision, but it IS a behaviour change and is flagged for confirmation. REQUIRING DECISIONS: ADM-77 (a lapsed quote can currently still be DECLINED, and moving the status silently removes that because the not_sent guard precedes the validity check), ADM-78 (whether lapsed is terminal, supersedable, extendable or revivable), ADM-79 (who is told). ALSO NOTED as remaining implementation scope, not a decision: once a row is lapsed the not_sent branch returns "A client can only answer a quotation that was actually sent to them", which is false of a quote that was sent and then lapsed - the same class of defect as G-101's refusal reason and the ADM-74 announcement line. CLOSED 2026-08-14. ADM-77, ADM-78 and ADM-79 were taken as DELEGATED decisions under the owner standing authorization, each recorded with its reasoning. A SEPARATE LIVE DEFECT was found while implementing and is fixed here: the not_sent outcome mapped to the message "A client can only answer a quotation that was actually sent to them", which was ALREADY FALSE of an accepted, rejected or superseded quote - every one of which WAS sent - and the branch that would have said "already answered" was UNREACHABLE, because the outcome implied the status was not sent. So answering an already-accepted quotation told the user it had never been sent. The outcome is now not_answerable and the message distinguishes answered, superseded and not-yet-sent. ALSO FOUND: npm run db:types used --linked and produced a types.ts missing ten symbols including handoffs, models and routing_policies; it silently corrupted the file when run, and now targets --local.
gaps.status: CLOSED - lapsed is a persisted state, and the three consequences are decided

The conflict this gap recorded is therefore resolved by ruling on the CREATION moment and leaving the START moment exactly as ADM-13 granted it. gaps.title: a claim of one could take the whole queue
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/verify-job-claims.mjs (36 live, 5 proved red against the unfixed function)
gaps.evidence: core.claim_jobs could claim every queued job of a kind in one statement, hand them all to one worker, and leave all but one stranded in running with their attempts spent - invisible to every other claim until the reaper released them fifteen minutes later. The mechanism: limit p_batch_size, where LIMIT NULL in Postgres means no limit. Not an error, not zero - every row. Measured: with four queued and a null batch size, claim_jobs returned 4, all sharing one locked_by and one locked_at. That is exactly the signature that failed verify-requirement-proposal section 8c four times in CI: two jobs, one worker id, one timestamp to the microsecond, one settled and one left running. Two separate transactions cannot share a locked_at - measured, they differ by microseconds - so identical values proved a single statement. Fixed by making the limit total: greatest(coalesce(p_batch_size, 1), 1). The coalesce restores the documented default for a null; the greatest refuses zero and negatives, which claimed nothing and reported an empty queue - the same lie in the other direction. The callers being correct was not accepted as the fix. A claim contract that says "up to N" must never be able to mean "all of them", whatever a caller, a driver, a schema cache or a future maintainer does with the argument. A live script now covers the claim itself, which had none of its own despite every queue depending on it: single worker, concurrent workers, one job and four workers, the lock, a crashed worker, lease recovery through the reaper, retries and the attempt budget, and dedupe_key idempotency.

gaps.title: one job queue starved another
gaps.testCoverage: scripts/verify-approval-announcements.mjs (18 live, one proved red against the unfixed runner)
gaps.evidence: Introduced by G-110 and found while investigating a CI failure it did not obviously cause. The announce drain returned early, copied from the unlock drain above it. Unlocks can afford that - milliseconds of pure database work - but an announcement reaches an outside provider, which makes it the same shape as the extraction path behind it. So a single queued announcement starved every later queue for that whole invocation: a tick answered claimed:1 kind:approval.announce and left requirement.extract at queued, attempts 0. Under cron the cost is one delayed tick; in CI, where the scripts drive the runner directly rather than waiting sixty seconds, it is the difference between a tick doing its work and none of it. The early return is removed and the tick falls through. The wall clock stays bounded: announcements share the unlock batch size and extraction claims exactly one job. A live check plants an announcement ahead of an extraction and asserts one tick reaches both - proved red against the unfixed runner first, and isolated from the script own approvals so it measures starvation rather than leftovers.

gaps.evidence: Found 2026-08-14 while planning the foundation. ADM-83 fixed the handoff shape and required the receiver to be an allowed target in the SENDER's registry definition, which bounds WHERE a handoff may go and not HOW FAR a chain runs. A -> B -> A -> B is legal under every rule now recorded: each hop is a valid target, each agent is within its autonomy, each step is audited. max_cost_minor bounds the damage in MONEY and not in TIME, and it stops the chain only after the budget is spent. A loop inside one correlation chain reads as progress - new handoffs, new runs, new steps - so nothing looks wrong while nothing advances. ENGINEERING DECISION, recorded as one rather than deferred as business policy: a depth bound is the same class of safety limit as a retry count, and the fail-safe direction is unambiguous - stop and escalate to a human. Scoped PER CORRELATION CHAIN, because the chain is already the unit of tracing in agent_runs. On reaching the bound the handoff becomes failed_permanent and escalates, which is the only outcome ADM-83 permits: silently completing with partial evidence is forbidden. The specific number is deliberately NOT fixed here - it belongs with the implementation, where it can be tested against a real chain rather than guessed in a plan. CLOSED 2026-08-14 with F3. The bound is 8, per correlation chain, enforced by a CHECK on ai.handoffs.depth and indexed by (correlation_id, depth). Eight is recorded in the migration WITH ITS REASONING rather than as a bare number: the longest legitimate chain the approved roster implies is requirement -> PM -> design -> prototype -> build -> QA -> handover, which is seven, so eight leaves one hop of headroom and still stops a two-agent loop on its fourth round trip. A number in a schema with no reasoning beside it is a number nobody can ever revise, because nobody knows what it was protecting.

gaps.title: the cron secret was compared with a plain operator
gaps.status: CLOSED - all three secret comparisons now go through one constant-time helper
gaps.implementationState: closed by src/lib/constant-time.ts; cron-auth.ts and whatsapp/verify.ts both import it and neither keeps a private copy
gaps.productionVerificationState: verified by unit test, not production. Behaviour is unchanged: the right header is accepted, a missing header is 401 rather than a crash, a bare secret and a differently-cased scheme are refused, and an unset secret is still 503 (disabled, not forbidden). gaps.evidence: Found 2026-08-14 by the pre-production security audit. The repository had THREE shared-secret comparisons and two were constant-time: authorizeSubscription (WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN) and authorizeSignature (the webhook HMAC) both used a private equals() in src/lib/whatsapp/verify.ts which documented the length-leak tradeoff explicitly. authorizeCronRequest compared the Authorization header with !==. What marked this as an oversight rather than a weighed decision is that cron-auth.ts documented everything ELSE about the comparison - that the header is compared whole so the Bearer scheme is required by construction, that an unset secret fails closed, that nothing logs or echoes the secret - and said nothing at all about timing. The route is publicly reachable (Vercel Cron calls it over the internet) and the secret grants job-queue execution. SEVERITY IS RECORDED HONESTLY AND IS LOW: remotely timing a JavaScript string comparison across the public internet is extremely difficult and network jitter swamps the nanosecond differences involved. This is defence in depth and consistency, not the closing of an exploited hole. It was worth doing because the primitive already existed, the cost is one function call, and a reader comparing the two edges would reasonably ask why they differ. The helper was extracted to src/lib/constant-time.ts rather than duplicated: two copies of a security primitive drift, and a private one invites the next edge to write != again because the safe version is not visible from where it is needed. The audit that found it also confirmed CLEAN: 44/44 tables have RLS, every SECURITY DEFINER function pins search_path, no policy is unconditionally true, no policy is reachable by anon or public, public.bootstrap_first_owner is a thin delegate to the core function carrying G-084's identity check rather than a stale duplicate, and core.alert_state's policy-less RLS is a deliberate deny-all that verify-operational-backlog.mjs check 6 already proves unreachable.

gaps.title: the handoff depth bound had no producer
gaps.evidence: Found 2026-08-14 alongside G-133. ai.handoffs.depth is default 0 with check (depth >= 0 and depth <= 8) and NOTHING DERIVED IT FROM ANYTHING. The CHECK constrained the number a caller writes, not the length of a chain - and the default is 0, so a caller that never sets it was never bounded. A to B to A to B could run forever with every row reading depth 0 and every constraint satisfied. Proved by dropping the trigger and inserting twelve handoffs in one correlation, every one passing depth 0: all twelve were accepted and all twelve stored 0. That is precisely the recursion the completion mandate's section 17 forbids. Depth is now derived by trigger as max(depth in the correlation chain) + 1, IGNORING what the caller passed, because a derived value a caller may override is a suggestion rather than a bound and the caller here is an agent. Per correlation chain rather than per parent branch: the stricter reading, matching what 20260814120003 already recorded as the unit of tracing, and needing no new column so nothing has to be backfilled. A named consequence: parallel handoffs consume depth even though they are not a chain, which bounds total work in a correlation rather than only the longest path.

gaps.title: nothing said which lead needed a person first
gaps.status: CLOSED - crm.lead_attention ranks live leads by recorded fact-tiers, and /leads opens with it
gaps.implementationState: Doc 09 section 31 asks for lead prioritisation and the owner's mandate gives it a number: 200-300 leads a month. At that volume the first question of the day is not 'what is my pipeline' but 'who is waiting for me', and /leads answered only the first. crm.lead_attention(limit, org) ranks live leads by TIER, most urgent first: handed_over (agent_paused_at set - the agent stopped and a person was promised), waiting_on_us (the newest message is the client's), quoted_no_answer (a proposal sent), ready_to_quote (an accepted requirement version with no proposal), open_objection (a concern whose response is null), never_answered, quiet. Within a tier, OLDEST FIRST - a client waiting three days outranks one waiting three minutes - with the lead id as a stable tie-break so the page does not shuffle between loads. NO SCORE, and that is ADM-88 rather than a preference: section 31 lists nine signals and section 10 ten dimensions with configurable weights, and ADM-88 refused all of it. There is no weight, no threshold and nothing to tune, so there is also nothing to explain when somebody disagrees with a placement - the reason is one word. Deliberately NOT consent-gated, unlike crm.reactivation_priority: that feeds an outbound queue and this feeds a person's morning, and a client who wrote to us yesterday must appear whether or not a consent row exists. A settled lead drops off. Migration 20260823190000.

gaps.title: two readers had an opinion about a message's language, and the column is written once
gaps.status: CLOSED - the intent read leaves a language somebody already heard alone
gaps.implementationState: Found on production by the first successfully transcribed voice note. A recording has TWO readers with an opinion about its language: the transcriber, which heard it, and the intent read, which reads a transcript of it. The transcriber writes first (crm.conversation_messages.language, set in markRead), so the intent read wrote second - and freeze_message_language refused it, correctly, taking the WHOLE intent read down with it. The message was therefore never labelled at all, and the job was on its way to burning five model calls to fail the same way each time. The freeze is right and the fix belongs in the caller: MESSAGE_INTENT now reads `language` alongside `intent` and omits it from the update when the column already holds a value. Whoever read it first read it from the thing itself; the intent read is reading a transcript of it, which is further away.

gaps.title: the approval announcement carrying a price was refused at the row, so the owner was never told
gaps.status: CLOSED - the announcement names the person who asked, and drops the number rather than the message when nobody did
gaps.implementationState: Found while auditing the quotation-to-close flow, and it sat directly in the path the owner was about to walk. announcementFor renders event.amountMinor as currency; crm.refuse_unread_price refuses an agency message stating a price when author_id is null. So the FIRST quotation ever submitted would have raised its approval, queued the announcement, and had the row refuse it - retrying until the job died with the owner never told anything at all. Nobody had hit it because nobody had submitted a quotation, and verify-approval-announcements tested the EVENT and never the MESSAGE. Two halves. Where a person asked - which is the real quotation path, since submitProposal passes context.userId to request_approval - the announcement is authored by them, read from approval_requests.requested_by_id rather than added to the event, and the guard is satisfied by being TRUE rather than by carving a hole in it. Where an agent asked, the AMOUNT is dropped and the message says an amount is inside: losing the whole notification to protect a number is the wrong trade, since the message exists to say something needs you and AgencyOS is one tap away.

gaps.title: "Send quotation" sent nothing — it marked a row and recorded a reference somebody typed
gaps.status: CLOSED - an approved quotation is composed and sent to the client, once
gaps.implementationState: sales.send_proposal never sent anything: it marked the row `sent`, took a p_message_ref the caller had typed, and returned. So 'Send quotation' meant 'I have sent this myself, note it down' - and on a deployment where nobody knew that, an approved quotation reached nobody. Doc 09 section 18 asks for the opposite: send it, record the timestamp, record the reference, link it to the conversation. sendProposal now composes the quotation (quotationMessage: title, version, summary, the priced lines, subtotal/discount/tax only where non-zero, total, validity only where set - nothing invented) and sends it through crm.sendClientMessage rather than around it, so consent, the sequence, the provider call and the delivery record are all its, and the message is AUTHORED BY WHOEVER PRESSED SEND - which is what carries a price past crm.refuse_unread_price. THE ORDER IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE: the message goes FIRST and send_proposal stamps the row after, because mark-then-send leaves a row saying sent with nothing sent whenever the provider refuses - the exact shape that made a refused reply unretryable in PR #300. Approval is checked twice: cheaply before anything can reach a client, and again under the row lock inside send_proposal, which is the one that counts. Idempotency is the key `proposal:<id>:v<version>` (section 28), so a second press answers already_sent and the client's phone stays quiet. The UI button said 'Mark as sent to the client' and meant it; it says 'Send to the client' now, and the reference field remains for a quotation that genuinely went another way.
gaps.productionVerificationState: NOT LIVE-VERIFIED, and stated rather than implied: the send runs behind an authenticated Server Action and no verification script holds a session, so it is proved against a stub. What is live-verified underneath it is crm.send_outbound_message, which every outbound path in this system already uses.

Two existing tests changed premise honestly rather than being loosened: an unapproved send is now refused BEFORE anything is sent, and its two distinct messages are kept.

gaps.title: The owner was asked to approve a price without being shown what it was for
gaps.status: CLOSED - the approval announcement carries the quotation, and the approval is still settled in AgencyOS
gaps.implementationState: Document 09 section 14 says the approver receives the quotation. What they received was a title, a total, a role and a reference - enough to know a decision existed, not enough to make one. The scope, which is the reviewable half, was only in AgencyOS: fine as a destination, wrong as a precondition, because an approval sits between the salesperson and the client and every minute of it is the client waiting. A total tells you how big a decision is; the lines tell you whether it is the right one - '70,000' carries no signal that the customer app was quoted and the driver app forgotten. ONE FIELD CHANGED IN THE DATABASE: sales.submit_proposal already builds the approval payload from the proposal it is holding, and now puts the line items in it (description, quantity, corrected amount, ordered by position then created_at so two announcements of one quotation read alike). Assembled there because that is where the proposal is, which lets the announcer render it without reaching across a module boundary into sales tables. The event was NOT widened - approval.requested still carries its seven facts and the handler reads the payload off the request row, where it already reads requested_by_id, because the row is the authority and an event shape is a second copy to keep in step. announcementFor renders the quotation for a proposal subject: title and version, what it covers, and subtotal/discount/tax ONLY where non-zero and validity ONLY where set - a zero read as a fact somebody entered is how an empty column becomes an invented one. Twelve lines maximum, and it SAYS how many it left out, because a silent truncation reads as a complete list and an owner approving a scope they believe they read in full is the failure this exists to prevent. The generated summary is dropped when the block already says it and a summary a person typed is kept. THE PRICE GUARD IS NOT WEAKENED AND NO EXEMPTION WAS ADDED: the rendered block states prices, so it sits behind the same authored gate as the amount always did. An agent-raised request keeps the priceless form - says an amount is involved, names no number, and lands - rather than being refused by crm.refuse_unread_price and never arriving. ADM-74 IS UNTOUCHED AND THAT IS THE POINT: the channel may deliver the request, carry its content and point at the reference; it may not settle the decision. Nothing here reads a reply, the wording still says 'Decide it in AgencyOS', and a test asserts the migration contains no path into decide_approval. What changed is that the owner arrives at AgencyOS knowing what they are about to approve instead of arriving to find out. D16: submit_proposal carried forward verbatim from 20260813120019 with the single marked edit.
gaps.productionVerificationState: PROVED AGAINST A REAL POSTGRES, NOT AGAINST PRODUCTION, AND THE REASON IS THE OWNER'S SETUP: production has no internal group linked and no approval policy, so no quotation has ever been submitted there and there is no channel for an announcement to land in. gaps.title: A quotation existed only as a chat message — nothing a client could keep
gaps.status: CLOSED - the quotation renders as a deterministic PDF; the owner's copy rides the approval announcement, the client's rides the send, and AgencyOS serves it on demand
gaps.implementationState: Brief section 12: the quotation must be professional, readable, structured, branded, versioned, traceable - and 'do not add undocumented commercial commitments'. What existed was a WhatsApp text (PR #321) that scrolls away; nothing a client saves, forwards or prints, and nothing the owner could review as the document the client would actually receive. THE RENDERER (src/lib/pdf/quotation.ts, pdf-lib + vendored Noto Sans): renders ONLY what the proposal rows record - zero discount is no Discount row, missing validity is no validity line, absent client is no PREPARED FOR block, empty body is not boilerplate; quantity appears only when not 1 and the QTY column only when it informs. DETERMINISTIC: the same record renders to the same bytes (metadata dates are the proposal's own created_at, nothing reads the clock), proved by byte-equality. STATUS-HONEST AND FAIL-CLOSED (ADM-76): only approved/sent/accepted render clean; every other status - including one the module has never heard of - carries a labelled band (FOR INTERNAL REVIEW / DRAFT / SUPERSEDED / EXPIRED), because a draft PDF that looks final IS final to whoever the client forwards it to. Every draw goes through one wrapper that records a drawnText transcript, which is what makes 'the document does not say Discount' assertable at all - the content streams are compressed CID glyph runs. FONTS: PDF's built-in fonts stop at WinAnsi, which has no rupee sign - the one glyph every money string in this application needs. Noto Sans vendored under OFL, PRE-SUBSET with fontTools at vendor time (38 kB per weight) and embedded WHOLE with subset:false, because pdf-lib's own at-embed-time subsetting produces fonts Apple's CoreGraphics renders with most glyphs missing - watched happen: the first render lost r, a, t and most digits under macOS sips while the same bytes were perfect in Chrome, and an iPhone opening a WhatsApp document IS CoreGraphics. next.config outputFileTracingIncludes ships the .ttf files into every serverless bundle; verified in the .nft.json trace manifests of both the download route and the jobs runner. THE DATABASE (migration 174, D16 carry-forward of crm.send_outbound_message from 20260815460000 with three marked edits): the transcript could not say a document was sent - the function took only a body and hardcoded its metadata. It now takes p_media_type/p_media_filename; a document row records an EMPTY body with metadata.media_type='document' plus filename, exactly the shape conversation_messages_body_check already permits, so NO constraint moved. Any other media claim answers bad_shape. Consent, idempotency on external_ref, sequence, routing, audit: carried forward verbatim and applying to documents unchanged. The inbound reading engine stays asleep by construction (awaits_media_reading wants image/audio plus media_id; an outbound document row has neither). THE OWNER'S COPY (handleApprovalRequested, second leg after the text announcement settles): external_ref approval:<id>:pdf, authored by requested_by_id, upload then document message via two new provider functions (uploadWhatsAppMedia answers Graph's top-level {id}, sendWhatsAppDocument names it - deliberately no caption, the words travel in the text message where crm.refuse_unread_price can read them). THE AUTHORED GATE IS THE HANDLER'S OWN: a PDF states prices, the DB cannot read a PDF, so an agent-raised request sends NO document and keeps G-155's priceless form - a service-owned guard, tested against the running app, per the guard-ownership discipline. Failure classes are section 27's: transient fails the job so the retry finishes the leg (each leg idempotent under its own key); renderer crash or permanent refusal records the failure and answers announced_without_pdf - the owner has the full text either way. THE CLIENT'S COPY (sendProposal third step): text first, then crm.sendClientDocument keyed proposal:<id>:v<n>:pdf, THEN the stamp - a transient document failure stops BEFORE send_proposal so the quotation stays approved and a retry can finish (a stamped quotation refuses the whole path, which would strand the PDF forever); a permanent refusal or render crash is said in the answer (pdfDelivered/pdfNote, surfaced by the action) and the stamp proceeds. sendClientDocument deviates from sendClientMessage twice, documented: provider failure is DATA (delivered:false + retryable) because its caller stamps by that difference, and already_sent re-attempts when the row is not sent - the resend PR #300 paid for. THE SCREEN: GET /api/quotations/[proposalId]/pdf - the repository's first authenticated file download; the service owns session, capability (lead.read, the same gate every proposal page uses), RLS reads and render; the route only translates to HTTP. A PDF link on every version in the lead page's quotation history, drafts included - reviewing a draft document is what the band is FOR. ADM-74 UNTOUCHED: the PDF into the internal group is content the channel may carry; nothing reads replies, the approval settles in AgencyOS. ADM-22 untouched: the document renders recorded prices, invents none. Dependencies added: pdf-lib 1.17.1 + @pdf-lib/fontkit 1.1.1, pure JS, no binaries.
gaps.productionVerificationState: THE OWNER LEG IS LIVE-PROVED against the local stack: scripts/verify-approval-announcements.mjs section 0b (13 new checks, 27 -> 40) plants a real lead/deal/quotation with items and a proposal approval policy, raises a person-authored proposal approval, and watches the app's own job runner deliver BOTH legs through a Graph stub that answers uploads with the upload shape: the document row lands with media_type document, a real filename, empty body, the author, delivery settled sent; the upload carries real bytes and the document message names the exact media id the upload answered - the two calls proved to be one delivery. THE CLIENT LEG AND THE DOWNLOAD are proved against stubs only (tests/quotations.test.ts section G with the REAL renderer running inside, tests/outbound-messages.test.ts section H), for G-154's unchanged reason: both run behind an authenticated session no verification script holds. gaps.title: A client asking to change a sent quotation left no row, no rank, and no script
gaps.status: CLOSED - the ask becomes an objection row, the attention queue says revision_asked, the agent keeps section 23's script, and drafting v2 turns the loop
gaps.implementationState: Brief sections 23/24: 'Add live tracking and reduce price to 55k' must become a STRUCTURED change request, a revised version, an owner approval, and v2 to the client - repeatably, with no one-revision assumption. Section 26's own instruction was 'do not create a duplicate state machine if one already exists', and almost the whole loop DID exist: the structured change request is a sales.objections row (section 19/20 - the client's exact words, the kind, the version it was raised against, open until a person answers); the revised version is draft_proposal's supersede (any live status including sent, approval cancelled through the engine, versions unbounded); the owner's review is the approval engine with the full quotation and its PDF (G-155/G-156); the owner's own revision path already existed too (rejection returns the proposal to draft via sync_proposal_decision); v2 to the client is send_proposal. The objections engine's OWN migration even recorded the honest limit this closes: 'a feature objection that arrives labelled something else is not noticed here.' FOUR CONNECTIONS, in one migration (175, two D16 carry-forwards) and one prompt file: (1) THE ASK BECOMES A ROW - crm.emit_objection_raised gains 'change_request' beside its original three intents, still only on the first labelling; INTENT_PROMPT tells the classifier that a message asking to change, add to, remove from or re-price a sent quotation is change_request on a lead as much as on a project; OBJECTION_PROMPT's feature kind now names 'asking to add or remove something from the scope'. (2) THE QUEUE TELLS THE TRUTH - crm.lead_attention gains revision_asked between waiting_on_us and quoted_no_answer: an OPEN objection against the version that is OUT with the client. A lead whose client answered the quotation with 'change it' sat in quoted_no_answer - a true count and a false sentence. The tier clears itself the honest way: drafting v2 supersedes v1 and the join on status='sent' stops matching. NOTHING writes into the objection's response column - the response is what a person actually said (ADM-76), and a test asserts the migration contains no such write. (3) THE PERSON CAN SEE IT - sales.objections was read by exactly one thing (the agent's own context file); the lead page now lists open objections in the client's words above the draft form, with the draft-form hint gated on the viewer actually holding proposal.draft; listOpenObjectionsForLead follows G-054. The leads screen names the tier 'Asked to change the quote'. (4) THE AGENT KEEPS SECTION 23'S SCRIPT - REPLY_PROMPT gains the standing rule (changes to a sent quotation are not yours to grant or refuse; acknowledge, say the team will confirm an updated quotation internally, promise nothing; NOT a hand-over), which covers the same-tick race where the reply composes before the objection row exists; salesFileFor says it again once the row exists, gated on an open objection AGAINST THE SENT VERSION - the same condition as the tier, so the queue and the agent's file never tell two different stories; and mid-loop the file names the version the client is actually holding (newest sent, not the first superseded row - three revisions in, that difference is v1 vs v3). DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT: no auto-drafted v2. The mandate's diagram feeds the change request straight into a generated revision, but drafting v2 SUPERSEDES the quotation the client is holding, and an agent retracting the standing offer on its own reading of one message is a decision, not a read (ADM-61 section 5, ADM-22). The row and the tier put the ask in front of a person; the person clicks draft; the owner approves; the loop turns.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED in scripts/verify-quotations.mjs section 15 (79 -> 89 checks) against the local stack, pure PostgREST with no app dependency: a quotation walked through the full engine dance (draft, price, submit, approve, send) reads quoted_no_answer; labelling the client's 'Add live tracking and make it 55k' as change_request emits objection.raised (the widened gate); the objection row against the sent version flips the lead to revision_asked, RANKED ABOVE a control lead whose sent quotation is merely unanswered; drafting v2 supersedes v1 and the tier clears to open_objection with the objection's response still null (ADM-76); v3 drafts as easily as v2 (section 24's no-one-revision rule). RED-PROVED TWICE against the live definitions: the change_request intent removed from the gate (the event check went red with 0 events) and the tier's join flipped to draft (the queue check went red reading exactly the old false sentence, quoted_no_answer). The second red-proof's first attempt did not apply - the mangle's assert failed loudly instead of the proof silently not running. gaps.title: The Set policy button never worked — a partial unique index cannot be PostgREST upsert's conflict target
gaps.status: CLOSED - approvals.set_policy states the partial predicate the upsert never could; the settings form's own door is live-proved as a minted owner
gaps.implementationState: Found by the OWNER, on production, on the exact five-minute setup step the section-44 report named as the gap between YELLOW and GREEN: 'Could not save the approval policy', every time, including the first. The rung-uniqueness rule is a PARTIAL index (one ACTIVE rung per organization/subject/amount, where active) so a deactivated rung does not block the next; the service wrote through PostgREST's upsert, which emits ON CONFLICT (cols) with no predicate; Postgres refuses to match a bare column list against a partial index (42P10) AT PLAN TIME, conflict or no conflict. The statement never once executed. Nothing caught it because every prover used a different door: live scripts planted policies with plain POSTs, unit tests mocked the client, and the form's own test stubbed the service - the half-a-check family, wearing a new coat: the one shape production runs ran nowhere. FIX: migration 176 adds approvals.set_policy (SECURITY INVOKER - RLS still admits only the organization's owner; the money floor stays in the constraint) doing the insert with `on conflict (organization_id, subject_type, min_amount_minor) where active do update`, which is the one syntax that can name a partial index. The service switched from .upsert to the rpc, maps a money-floor refusal to the honest VALIDATION sentence, and treats a non-saved outcome as FORBIDDEN. The 'setting the same subject and amount again replaces that rung' promise the page makes is now true.
gaps.productionVerificationState: REPRODUCED FIRST: the exact supabase-js upsert shape (on_conflict + resolution=merge-duplicates) against the local stack answers 42P10 byte-for-byte the production failure. gaps.title: the quotation refuses its own defects: the corpus study becomes controls, themes and the clauses that were missing
gaps.status: CLOSED - the owner's study of all 45 sent quotations turned into enforcement: the arithmetic gate at the render boundary, the language gate at the write, one brand with twelve industry accents, the four commercial clauses the corpus effectively did not have, and a regulated-category backstop a model cannot opt out of
gaps.implementationState: The owner read all 45 quotation PDFs sent 29 Jul - 22 Aug 2026 (32 engagements) and the study counted what actually shipped. TWO DEFECT CLASSES, both enforced now, at DIFFERENT LAYERS on purpose. (1) ARITHMETIC: five documents carried a cost table that did not sum to its own total - DharmikIndia by Rs5,40,000 on a Rs19,75,000 quotation, Tango's two by Rs5,000 and Rs10,000, Kaka Plastic's by Rs15,000, Smart PG's grand total holding only because a subtotal was overstated by Rs1,000. The DATABASE already owns this invariant (sales.proposal_totals() re-sums the subtotal, proposals_total_is_arithmetic asserts subtotal-discount+tax=total), so quotationArithmeticFault() is deliberately NOT a duplicate of it: it covers what the database cannot see, that the items reach the renderer through a SEPARATE query from the totals and 'items ?? []' would paint a Total with no lines under it. It throws before a single glyph; all three doors already answer INTERNAL on a render throw. (2) LANGUAGE: priced lines promised 'structure ready', 'API-ready', 'hooks' and 'Much more Screens' without once saying what does not work at handover. PRICING_KNOWLEDGE has ASKED for this since ADM-96 and the corpus is the evidence that asking is not refusing - so quotationLanguageFault() REFUSES, in quotationScopeSchema at the WRITE, never at render, because an approved quotation is a record of what the owner decided and refusing to draw it later would break history to punish it. Three rules: an unbounded promise inside a fixed price (much more / and more / etc), a readiness word without a limit clause anywhere on its line, and a rupee figure written into prose (the price fields are the ones the arithmetic is checked on; percentages are deliberately NOT refused, because '20% off coupons' is a product feature and a false refusal fails the whole drafting job). THEMES: one master brand, twelve industry accents, and a theme may change exactly one thing - the accent hue at three fixed places (header keyline, section labels, the rule above the total). No section, no number, no sentence varies; the status band is deliberately unthemed because a warning that changes colour by industry is a warning nobody learns to read. An untheme'd or unknown-theme document renders BYTE-IDENTICAL to before, asserted against real bytes. SECTIONS the corpus was missing, all optional so an older model answer still drafts: dependencies (the sixth scope state, scattered in ~14/45), acceptanceCriteria (generalised from the only 8 documents that had it - the DharmikIndia phases), optionalAddons (one price each, never a range, drawn under 'OPTIONAL - NOT IN THE TOTAL ABOVE'), industryTheme and regulatedCategory. COMMERCIAL_TERMS states the four the corpus effectively did not have: acceptance was undefined in 42/45, cancellation in 1/45, a liability cap in 1/45, jurisdiction named in 3/45; VALIDITY_DAYS gives the 15-day modal one home. REGULATORY is the sharpest one: the corpus disclaimed licensing well on the casino quotation and RBI/NBFC on all three lending ones, then shipped a wagering quotation with operator-controlled result and payout-ratio settings and no regulatory sentence at all - so regulatedCategoriesFor() takes the model's declaration UNION what the scope's own words show and can only ADD, never remove. All three render doors now pass the scope text so the backstop reads the quotation's own lines. NO MIGRATION: every new field lives inside the existing proposals.document jsonb, already frozen outside draft by proposals_guard. The enumerated section spread at the three doors was replaced by ...(sections ?? {}) - it meant three edits per new section and three chances to forget one.

gaps.title: the price checks itself against the lane: the corpus formula in code, and the day-rate floor that could not work
gaps.status: CLOSED - the lane formula is executable, the model's proposed price is compared against it, and the difference is shown to the approver on the copy that already says NOT APPROVED. The corpus study's day-rate floor was PROVED vacuous against this engine and deliberately not built.
gaps.implementationState: TWO PARTS. (1) The corpus study proposed blocking any draft implying under Rs2,000 per developer-day against its own timeline band. That control is vacuous HERE and the tests prove it arithmetically rather than asserting it: timelineBandFor derives the timeline FROM the price, so the implied day-rate is a function of price alone and never sees scope. OTT (a Netflix-class platform at Rs50,000) and NearServe (a three-role marketplace at Rs50,000) imply the IDENTICAL Rs1,667/day - and OTT was the document the floor was proposed to catch. It would also refuse the corpus modal price (Rs50,000, 9/45), and it is not monotonic: Rs49,999 implies Rs3,333/day and Rs50,000 implies Rs1,667/day because the band steps 3-6wk to 6-9wk. Not built, and the reasoning is written into pricing-reference.ts so it is not proposed again next quarter. (2) What separates OTT from NearServe is the LANE - OTT is Lane 3 scope sold at the Lane 1 anchor - so pricing-reference.ts implements the formula PRICING_KNOWLEDGE has carried as prose since ADM-96, and nothing had ever checked the model against. laneReferenceFor counts surfaces (a surface is something a person opens; the backend, the design and the testing lines are excluded, because counting them would double every estimate), reads depth from the words with standard as the honest default, and applies the corpus levers: extra surfaces, the depth multiplier, API-ready/hooks, live integration, real-money mechanics, and native iOS ONLY when it is a separate deliverable (iOS on the same Flutter build stays Rs0, as this agency has always priced it). Lane 0 carries the owner-declared Rs20,000-Rs35,000 rule guarded by SCOPE rather than by the wish - one surface, no live integration. Lane 3 is reached by SUBJECT (a game, streaming or AI block changes the lane, not a line - the rule the fit uncovered) or by size, and is priced per surface. Every reference rounds to Rs5,000, like 45/45 of the corpus headlines. ADVISORY, NEVER BLOCKING: ADM-96 and ADM-07 put the number with the owner, and the module reads prose with regexes, so a false positive that blocked a draft would fail a whole job for a guess (G-164, paid for in production). The threshold is 30%, deliberately outside the fit's own 17.5% median error, so silence is the common case. STRUCTURALLY INTERNAL: the renderer draws the note only when statusBandFor already returns a band, so it can reach a draft or pending-approval copy and NOTHING a client receives - approved, sent and accepted cannot carry it whatever a caller passes.
