All 45 corpus quotations had a short reference a client could quote back (BE/EDU/2026/0813, BE-HRX-2026-0818, EHSAAS-MID-002) and the generated document had none. quotationReferenceCode is DERIVED, never allocated: a pure function of the proposal id and its prepared date, so it is stable for the life of the quotation, identical on every re-render, and needs no table, no sequence and no migration - and owes no answer about what happens to a discarded draft. It is deliberately NOT sequential and the tests say so: the year makes it sayable, six hex characters make it unambiguous across ~16.7M quotations in a year. It draws FIRST in the meta line, ahead of the version; the UUID stays in the footer. This is the name, that is the address. STATED AND NOT BUILT: the contact block (email, phone, location) that every corpus quotation carried and the generated PDF still lacks - a client who forwards the document cannot reach the agency from it. That needs new organization settings keys, and the whitelist is enforced IN THE DATABASE by set_organization_setting, so it needs a migration rather than a field. Named here rather than half-built.
gaps.productionVerificationState: NOT STARTED - no migration, no RPC, no new DB surface; a pure function and one drawn line.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-phase-names-what-it-defers.test.ts suite C (4): derived and stable across re-renders, explicitly NOT a counter, a malformed date degrades to a code rather than a crash, and the rendered document carries the sayable code at the top while the traceable UUID survives in the footer.

gaps.title: the document says who to call
gaps.status: CLOSED - the quotation PDF carries a contact block under the agency name, set by the owner and never invented
gaps.implementationState: Every one of the 45 quotations the corpus study read carried a contact block - an email, a phone number and a place. The generated PDF carried the agency NAME and nothing else, so a client who forwards it to a partner (which is the whole reason a PDF exists rather than a WhatsApp message) had no way to reach the agency from the document in their hand. G-170 named this and did not build it because the settings whitelist is enforced IN THE DATABASE; migration 182 widens it properly. Three new non-secret keys - quotation_contact_email, quotation_contact_phone, quotation_contact_location - go through the same door as the two that already existed, for the same reasons: the whitelist lives in core.set_organization_setting so no key can be smuggled in from a caller, each value is shaped on the way in because a typo on a client-facing document is caught cheaply there and expensively later, and the write is audited. Nothing about it widens what MAY be written - only which non-secret operational keys are recognised, and a probe against the live function confirms an api_key is still refused as invalid_key. THE GUARD TRAVELS WITH THE WHITELIST or it stops guarding: org_setting_write_is_sanctioned previously repeated each key in its own condition, which is exactly how a whitelist and its guard come to disagree, so both halves now read ONE array. The renderer draws the block under the name and above the keyline, where a letterhead puts it, and the module rule decides the rest: NOTHING IS INVENTED, so an unset block draws nothing at all and the document is byte-identical to before. quotationContactLine lives in the renderer module because BOTH doors need the same answer - the owner download and the copy the client is sent must not disagree about how to reach the agency. Settings page gains one form for the three keys, because they are one block on the document.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LOCAL: migration 182 applied to the local stack and the real core.set_organization_setting probed directly - a valid email, a phone with spaces and a leading +, and a location all accepted; a malformed email and a phone containing letters both refused invalid_value; an anthropic_api_key still refused invalid_key. NOT run against production, which has no contact keys set and will simply render no contact line until an owner sets them.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-document-says-who-to-call.test.ts (13): the block assembled from what is set and never from what is not (all three, subsets, nothing, non-object, and an unrelated setting that must not leak); on the page under the name, reaching the CLIENT copy while the approver note does not; the migration pins (three keys whitelisted, each shape-checked, the guard reading ONE array so the halves cannot drift, and no secret let through); and both doors reading the same settings. RED-PROVED by forcing a default contact line - which exposed that the first version of the absence test compared two equally-wrong renders and passed clean; rewritten to assert the absence positively, and the same red-proof then failed it correctly.

gaps.title: the reflex has a price: what the anchor costs, recorded at the decision and reported
gaps.status: CLOSED - every quotation records the formula's reading of its own shape beside the price the owner decided, and the sales funnel reports the gap
gaps.implementationState: The corpus study's sharpest commercial finding was that this agency prices onto round anchors and bends the scope to meet them: Rs50,000 bought an app plus an admin panel, a dual-app ERP, a three-role marketplace AND a Netflix-class OTT platform. That is a reflex, and a reflex cannot be argued with until somebody can see what it costs. THE DESIGN DECISION, which is the whole gap: the delta is RECORDED at draft time rather than recomputed on demand. The measurement is of a DECISION, so the figure has to be the one that was in front of the decider; recomputing later answers a different question - what today's formula says about an August quotation - which is a re-judgement with hindsight rather than a record. The formula has already moved once (G-169 gave it stated surfaces and depth), which is exactly the drift that would have silently rewritten history. storedReferenceFor writes lane, referenceRupees, proposedRupees, surfaces and depth into proposals.document at draft time, where proposals_guard freezes it the moment the quotation leaves draft. proposedRupees rides along deliberately: it duplicates the total, and that is the point, because a reference is only meaningful against the number it was compared to and a later revision must not silently re-baseline an old delta. All three drafting doors record it. getPricingReflex READS what was recorded and never re-derives it (a test asserts the funnel module does not even import the calculator); a quotation drafted before this existed is ABSENT from the measurement rather than a zero in it, because counting old rows as no-gap would dilute what is being measured; only quotations priced BELOW the reference are summed, because netting the two would hide the thing. Refuses on a failed read rather than coalescing to zero (G-054). The sales funnel - whose own copy already says it reports what happened and does not estimate - gains one section, and its wording is load-bearing: a gap is named as the cost of a DECISION, not an error, because the owner may have had every reason and a page that calls it a mistake would be both wrong and ignored. NO MIGRATION: the document column has held this shape since G-165. A TYPE ALIAS rather than an interface for StoredPricingReference, because only aliases get an implicit index signature and the value is written into a jsonb column typed as Json.
gaps.productionVerificationState: NOT STARTED - no migration, no RPC, no new DB surface. Pure functions plus one read through the existing client, and the write rides the document the three drafting workflows already update.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-reflex-has-a-price.test.ts (11): the record carries BOTH numbers rather than a bare gap, survives the document parse, and is written by all three drafting doors against the model's own lines; the reader takes what was recorded and provably does not import the calculator, treats a pre-G-172 quotation as absent rather than zero, sums only what is below, and refuses on a failed read; the page shows the section only once something is measured, names the gap as a decision rather than an error, says which reference it quotes, and states zero-below plainly. RED-PROVED twice: neutering the absence guard fails one, and removing the schema declaration fails the round-trip - which is how the round-trip test was found to be dishonest in the first place, since its  fallback had been passing while zod silently stripped the field on every parse.

gaps.title: the agent is told what it may write: seven fields were dead in production
gaps.status: CLOSED - the drafting prompts now name every field added since G-165, and the live verifier asserts they reach the row
gaps.implementationState: FOUND BY TESTING THE AGENT, not by reading. A drafted document was caught mid-flight on the local stack and carried every G-165 field and NONE of the seven added since: dependencies, acceptanceCriteria, optionalAddons, industryTheme, regulatedCategory (G-167), depth and phase (G-169). The schema accepted them, the assembler read them, the renderer drew them - and nothing told the model they existed, so QUOTATION_PROMPT still listed only (a)-(e) from G-165. Four merged changes had shipped features that could never fire. G-169 was the worst of it: its whole point was that STATED surfaces and depth beat prose inference, and the stored reference showed surfaces:3 depth:standard both INFERRED, so the fix was inert on every quotation. Only the code-written parts survived - the pricing reference (G-172), the regulated backstop, the arithmetic and language gates - because none of them asks the model for anything. THE FIX names each field WITH ITS CONSEQUENCE, because a field a model cannot see the point of is a field it leaves empty: kind is marked because the reference COUNTS surfaces and a backend counted as one inflates the figure the owner is shown; depth is stated because it moves a price x1.1 to x1.4 in this agency's own history; a deferral must name the LATER phase that owns it because that is what turns "why isn't X there?" into "X is phase 5". Applied to ALL THREE drafting prompts - the scope job and both revision paths - because telling one of three would leave two thirds of drafts empty. THE DEEPER MISS was in the verification, not the code: verify-quotation-scope checked that a document RIDES the row and never what was IN it beyond the G-165 fields, which is how the gap survived four merges and a full CI run. It now asserts every field lands, including that the reference counted the STATED surfaces rather than the prose.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE: verify-quotation-scope 35/35 (was 29/29; six new checks). RED-PROVED by emptying the model stub of the new fields, which reproduces the pre-fix world exactly - the same five checks go red reporting the same "(none)" the live inspection showed - then restored green. The whole agent set re-run on the same stack: quotation-dispatch 55/55, quotations 89 checks, sales-funnel 33/33, requirement-proposal, and the four agent scripts.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-reflex-has-a-price.test.ts suite D (4): every field added since G-165 is named in the prompt, all THREE drafting prompts carry it rather than just the first, the prompt states WHY the kind matters rather than only that it exists, and the live verifier asserts the fields actually land.

gaps.title: the agents drain together: one job per minute was the ceiling
gaps.status: CLOSED - the runner drains a bounded batch of agent jobs per tick instead of exactly one
gaps.implementationState: MEASURED, not argued. The runner claimed exactly ONE agent job per invocation and cron runs once a minute, so ten queued agent jobs took ten minutes and a busy morning queued faster than it drained. Eight enabled agents were not slow at their work - they were standing in a queue for it. Red-proved by forcing the batch back to 1: six queued jobs yielded claimed:1 from one tick; restored, the same six yielded claimed:6. The comment that held the old limit in place was not wrong, it was incomplete - "claiming more would leave rows running that nothing in this tick will settle" is true of an UNBOUNDED loop. This one is bounded twice: by a count (AGENT_BATCH) against a pathological queue, and by a wall-clock budget (AGENT_BUDGET_MS, 45s of a 60s window) which is the bound that actually matters because agent jobs make model calls and their duration varies by an order of magnitude. The budget is checked BEFORE each claim, never after, because a claimed row the tick abandons is running with an attempt spent and invisible until the reaper; and it is measured from the START of the tick because the reap, dispatch, unlock and announcement stages have already spent part of the same minute. The agent block became runOneAgentJob: every branch that used to answer the HTTP request now returns the same fact as a value, because a batch cannot return early on behalf of the jobs behind it. A NEW INVARIANT the single-job shape never needed: claimed.job is CLEARED once a job settles - left pointing at a finished job, a throw while claiming the next one would fail a row that had already succeeded. THE HONEST COST: the response now describes a batch, so three live verifiers that read the agent and reason at the top level went red. Each was updated to read agentRuns, and one was made STRONGER - the starvation check asserted the newer job was still queued, which was only ever a proxy for oldest-first ordering; with a batch that ordering is directly visible in agentRuns and is now directly asserted.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE on the local stack: the full agent set re-run green after the change - quotation-scope 35/35, quotation-dispatch 55/55, quotations 89 checks, requirement-proposal, agent-dispatch, agent-autonomy, agent-ceilings, agent-definitions, sales-funnel. The drain rate itself was measured directly against the running app (1 job/tick before, 6 after) rather than inferred.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-agents-drain-together.test.ts (7): the batch is bounded by BOTH a count and a wall-clock budget, the budget fits inside a cron minute and the count is greater than one, the budget gates the CLAIM rather than following it, the stamp precedes the batch; and one job's failure is not the batch's - runOneAgentJob answers with values not responses, every refusal reason survives, a failed claim mid-batch keeps the work already done, and the response reports a count. Plus tests/runner-throw.test.ts gains the cleared-claim invariant.

gaps.title: a verification that can only pass once: flow-01 replayed its own fixtures and went quiet
gaps.status: CLOSED - flow-01 keys every provider id per run, registers what the INGEST created, and clears what an earlier run left; a fleet test holds the rule for every script that plants a message
gaps.implementationState: FOUND BY A FRESH ZERO-TRUST AUDIT, not by CI, and CI is the reason. verify-flow-01 delivered its webhook messages under ids built from a CONSTANT marker - wamid.zztest-flow01.human.1, the same string every run - and crm.ingest_whatsapp_message is idempotent on that id, correctly, because that is what stops Meta's redeliveries duplicating a customer's words. So the FIRST run on a database stored the message and every run after it was a replay. A replay does not error: the script's sender number is fresh each run, so the ingest created a contact, a lead and an EMPTY conversation, appended nothing, emitted no message.received, queued no reply.compose, and section P waited sixty ticks for a pause nothing was going to write. CI builds its database from migrations, so the first run is the only run and it always passes; the rot is visible only on a database that has run the script before, which is every developer's machine and none of CI. Green pipeline, red laptop, for eight days. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY UNVERIFIED for those eight days: the agent handing a conversation to a person, the agent then staying silent, the escalation reaching the internal channel, and the announcement carrying the agent's own reason - sections P and Q were the only checks in the repository covering any of it, and the code they guard was fine the whole time. THE SECOND HALF, and the reason it could never self-heal: sections P and Q reach the database through the webhook, so their contact, lead and conversation are made by the ingest - invisible to a cleanup that only knew what it had inserted itself. Three rows were left behind on every run, including the two from 24 August that no cleanup had ever been able to reach. THE FIX IS THREE PARTS. A per-run token in every provider id (const RUN, and one wamid() helper so no caller can build one by hand and miss it). Registration of the ingest-created fixtures, placed BEFORE the assertions so a FAILING run still tidies up - debris is what makes the next run fail worse. And a preflight sweep of residue from an earlier run, scoped to contacts this script names after itself, because a fix that needs somebody to hand-delete rows first is not a fix. NOT A PRODUCT CHANGE: no application code, migration or schema was touched.
gaps.productionVerificationState: PROVED BY RE-RUNNING, which is the only proof that means anything here: verify-flow-01 run TWICE CONSECUTIVELY against a database that already held its fixtures, 61 checks green both times, and zero rows left behind after (contacts like zztest-flow01% = 0, conversation_messages like wamid.zztest-flow01% = 0). Section P now reports all thirteen of its checks green including the announcement leaving on the wire and addressed to the internal channel rather than the client. The blast radius was measured rather than assumed: eleven other verifiers that plant or read inbound messages were each run twice in a row - receipts, media, journey, proposal, ingest, webhook, announce, quotedispatch, quotations, chain, funnel - and all eleven passed both runs, so flow-01 was the only script with the defect. RED-PROVED TWICE: the run token removed from the helper (fleet check and the helper check both go red), and the ingest-fixture registration removed (both registration checks go red); restored, six of six pass.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/a-verification-that-can-only-pass-once.test.ts (6): the fleet is found at all so an empty sweep cannot pass, every script that plants inbound messages either drops its own tenant or keys every provider id per run, the run token exists and no provider id is built outside the helper, the ingest-created fixtures are registered, registration happens BEFORE the assertions, and a poisoned database heals itself. The run-uniqueness rule resolves each interpolated identifier against the SCRIPT'S OWN source rather than judging by name - verify-flow-01 writes const MARKER = 'zztest-flow01' (a constant wearing a variable's spelling, which is why this was invisible) while verify-delivery-receipts writes const MARK = `zzrcpt-${randomUUID()...}` (a variable with almost the same name and the opposite property), and a rule that judged by name would have called one of them wrong. Comments are stripped with codeOnly first: the docblock quotes the broken shape verbatim.

gaps.title: an approval nobody was told about: the silence settled as a success
gaps.status: CLOSED - an unannounced approval is counted and named failing, linking a channel announces what was already waiting, and a malformed event can no longer kill an announcement
gaps.implementationState: FOUND BY A ZERO-TRUST AUDIT reading the live database rather than the code. handleApprovalRequested resolves the organization's internal channel and, with none linked, returns { status: 'succeeded', outcome: 'no_group' }. The job settles GREEN: no dead job, no stalled job, no unpublished event, nothing core.operational_backlog counted. A quotation the agent drafted, priced and submitted sat at pending_approval indefinitely and the only way anybody found it was by opening /approvals and happening to look. THE BRANCH IS RIGHT AND WAS LEFT ALONE: an organization with no channel has nowhere to send, and failing the job would retry into the same absence until it parked dead - a configuration gap dressed up as a system fault. Only the silence was wrong. TWO HALVES. (1) COUNT IT: operational_backlog gains unannounced_approvals and oldest_unannounced_at - pending, internal-audience requests in an organization with no live internal channel of EITHER kind. Classed failing rather than degraded, and that is the judgement: overdue_approvals is degraded because a person has not answered, which is a person problem; this is the system never having asked one, and until somebody links a channel nothing is coming. The function is DROPPED and recreated because Postgres refuses to change a return type - caught at apply time, which is where the migration first failed. (2) FIX IT ON LINK: crm.announce_waiting_approvals re-emits approval.requested for every still-pending internal request, called by BOTH linkers after the link lands (never before - an announcement emitted while the channel does not yet exist is a job that answers no_group, the exact silence being fixed). Only for internal_group, never for a project group: emitting an internal approval at a client's thread is the one mistake this area exists to prevent. NOT security definer, deliberately - it takes an organization id, and a definer function reading approval requests for an id it was handed is a cross-tenant read waiting to be found; under the caller's own RLS an owner passing another tenant's id selects nothing. Free of duplicates by construction rather than by a new rule: the announcer keys its message on approval:<request id>. A SECOND DEFECT FOUND IN THE SAME LOG: 'jobs/dead approval.announce attempts 1 - malformed approval.requested payload: expected object, received undefined - parked dead'. The handler parsed the EVENT and killed the announcement permanently when the parse failed. An outbox event is insertable over PostgREST by an org owner (PR #178), so an unparseable payload is evidence about the event and none about the approval, which may be real and waiting. Every announcement fact now comes off approval_requests - the doctrine dispatchApprovedQuotation has followed since ADM-96: the row is the authority, the payload only says which row. A vanished request is a success (gone); a job naming no request at all is still permanent, because there is no row to read.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED end to end by scripts/verify-unannounced-approvals.mjs against the running app, 19 checks: the backlog answers with the column, a pending internal approval in a channel-less organization raises the count from its baseline and reports how long it has waited, the announce job still settles succeeded and sends nothing, linking the owner's number emits a SECOND approval.requested, the owner is finally told, the message is keyed approval:<id>, the count returns to baseline, re-announcing writes one message not two, a client-audience request adds nothing, and a tenant with no internal request announces nothing. RED-PROVED TWICE against the LIVE definitions, with pg_proc evidence printed before and after each: the count replaced by a hard-coded zero (section 2 goes red, 0 -> 0) and the announce-on-link call stripped from crm.link_internal_recipient (section 4 goes red, 1 event, 0 messages). Restored, 19/19 green. The script owns two organizations and resets them at both ends - approvals.reject_delete refuses to delete an approval request under any circumstances, so a tenant that has raised one can never be dropped, and a fresh slug per run would leave an undeletable organization behind every time. Proved re-runnable by running it twice.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/an-approval-nobody-was-told-about.test.ts (21): an unannounced approval is failing while an overdue one is degraded, the sentence names the fix (no internal WhatsApp channel linked) rather than the symptom, the two are told apart and ordered worst-first, the alert fingerprint moves so the alert can fire at all, a clean backlog stays clean; the count is scoped to pending + internal + neither channel kind, and the same predicate appears THREE times - count, oldest, and the announcer - so the page cannot report an approval that linking would never announce; the drop precedes the create; both linkers announce and the project group does not; the announcement follows the link; announce_waiting_approvals is not security definer and pins its search_path; the re-emitted payload carries all seven fields; the handler selects every fact off the row, no longer parses the event, answers gone for a vanished request, keeps the permanent refusal only for a job naming no request, and the no_group branch is unchanged; and the operations page counts it separately in a widened grid. tests/approval-announcements.test.ts gains four: a malformed payload is announced from the row, a payload with no event at all is announced, a job naming no request is still permanent, and a vanished request is gone.

gaps.title: the timeline is a promise, not a formula: the one field of a quotation nobody could change
gaps.status: CLOSED - the model proposes a timeline band, the owner's note can change it, and an absent one still falls back to the corpus band exactly as before
gaps.implementationState: FOUND BY TRACING ONE SENTENCE an owner might realistically write on a revision: 'Price 50,000 se 45,000 kar do aur timeline 25 days se 20 days.' The price half worked exactly as designed. The timeline half had NOWHERE TO GO. timelineBandFor(totalMinor) derived the weeks from the price across five bands, so the timeline was the one field of a quotation nobody - not the model, not the owner, not the client - could change; the reviser applied every other instruction in the note and dropped that one without saying so, and the document came back with the same band unless the new price happened to cross a band edge. The drafting prompts said so out loud: 'Payment schedules, timelines, support terms and GST are written by the system from standing policy - never by you.' The model was told not to have an opinion about the one thing a client asks about first. THE SHAPE OF THE FIX: timelineWeeks is a BAND and never a date, because the corpus quotes a band and never a date (45/45) and because TIMELINE_TERMS's three sentences about when the clock starts only make sense beside one. The object is STRICT, so a model answering with deliverBy is refused rather than quietly stripped - a date is the one thing a client will hold the agency to that this document deliberately does not promise. STATED BEATS DERIVED, the same order of authority G-169 gave surfaces and depth: absent, timelineBandFor answers exactly as before, so every quotation drafted before this field existed renders identically and an APPROVED one keeps the timeline it was approved with rather than acquiring a new one when the price band moves underneath it. Three defensive details, each with a reason: the stored value is re-checked at render because it has been through a jsonb column and a backwards range on a client's quotation is cheap to refuse; the document field carries .catch(null) because z.number() refuses a null or a NaN and without it ONE bad timeline would make the entire document unparseable, losing the understanding, the exclusions and the assumptions with it; and the assembler falls back rather than throwing, because the fallback band is never wrong. THE APPROVER IS TOLD, and only when it matters: timelineNoteFor says nothing while the stated weeks OVERLAP the band the price implies, and speaks only when they do not touch - faster than the band is a promise somebody has to keep, slower is a reason a client may go elsewhere, and the two get different sentences because they are different problems. Silence is the common case on purpose, the same posture pricingNoteFor takes about price. Two approver notes are now possible on one quotation, so the renderer splits them into separate items rather than joining them into one run-on paragraph. THE PROMPTS: all three drafting prompts name TIMELINE with why it matters (the G-173 lesson - a field a model is never told about is a field it leaves empty), the sentence claiming the system writes it is gone from all three while its true neighbours survive, the revision prompt says the owner's note may change it and what to do when the note is silent, and both revisers are SHOWN the current timeline because that instruction is unfollowable otherwise.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED at both ends against the running app. verify-quotation-scope (36 checks, was 35): the timeline the model proposed reaches the row - 4-5 weeks, deliberately outside the band the price implies so the approver note fires too. verify-quotation-dispatch (56 checks, was 55): the owner's note now reads 'Price the driver app at 20000, add onboarding support, aur timeline 3 weeks kar do' and the revision comes back carrying 3-3 weeks - the exact sentence the audit traced, working end to end. RED-PROVED TWICE: the stated-beats-derived preference removed from quotationSectionsFor (4 of 25 tests go red) and one of the three TIMELINE prompt paragraphs deleted (1 goes red); restored, 25/25.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-timeline-is-a-promise-not-a-formula.test.ts (25): the schema takes a band of whole weeks, refuses one that ends before it starts, refuses a delivery date outright, and stays optional; the document round-trips it; stated beats derived; an absent one renders the IDENTICAL label at six different totals spanning all five bands, which is the backward-compatibility claim asserted rather than assumed; a backwards or nonsensical stored band falls back rather than printing itself; the page draws the stated weeks with the clock-starts sentence still beside them; the approver note is silent while the bands overlap, silent with nothing stated, differently worded for faster and slower, names the decision as the owner's, and reaches the approver block; the renderer draws two notes as two items and never lets a newline through the drawer; the approver block still never reaches a client; all three prompts name the timeline, none still claims the system writes it, the reviser is told the note may change it and is shown the one it must keep, all three doors persist it, and the wire schema declares it WITHOUT the integer bounds constrained decoding refuses (G-164).

gaps.title: the quotation says what it is made of: who uses it, and whose bill each service is
gaps.status: CLOSED - a quotation declares its roles, marks each line with the roles it serves, and names every third-party service with whose bill it is
gaps.implementationState: THE ZERO-TRUST AUDIT'S LARGEST FUNCTIONAL FINDING. The brief asks a quotation to identify modules, user roles, backend, frontend, admin, integrations and third-party dependencies; quotationScopeSchema had a flat list of priced lines and no way to express any of it. A role could appear only as prose inside a description, which made the commonest scope dispute in the corpus unrepresentable - 'we thought the admin could do that too'. And there was no third-party section at all: a gateway's percentage, a Play Store fee and an SMS rate could be mentioned in an exclusion or nowhere, and nowhere is what a fixed-price quotation that turns out to exclude the gateway's cut looks like at go-live. THREE DECISIONS WORTH DEFENDING. (1) NO PARALLEL MODULES TAXONOMY: items already describe the work, and a second list beside them would be two descriptions of one thing that drift. What was missing is the AUDIENCE, so each line names the roles it serves and the module-by-role matrix falls out of the structure that already exists. (2) SERVES IS A COLUMN, NOT ANOTHER JSONB KEY: it is a property of a LINE, and lines live in sales.proposal_items with features beside them for exactly this reason; putting it in the document would have required a second copy of every description to hang it off. add_proposal_item is DROPPED and recreated rather than replaced, because create-or-replace with a different argument list makes an OVERLOAD and a six-argument call is then ambiguous - a runtime error at the first draft rather than a failure at apply time. (3) NO PRICE FIELD FOR A THIRD-PARTY SERVICE: a gateway's percentage and a store's annual fee move, and neither is the agency's to promise; a figure printed inside a fixed-price quotation becomes a commitment nobody made. `charge` is free text so the model can write what the requirements actually established and nothing when they established nothing; `whoPays` is the enum, because whose bill it is is the part that causes the argument. THE REFERENTIAL RULE: a line may only name a role the quotation DECLARED, checked in the schema with a case-insensitive comparison (admin and Admin are one person; refusing over capitalisation would be a rule about typing rather than about scope). A model naming an audience it never defined has invented a user, and a quotation that invents a user has invented scope - the client reads it, agrees to it, and asks for it at handover. The two failures get different sentences because they are different mistakes: a typo names the roles that do exist, a quotation with no roles at all is told so. ON THE PAGE: WHO USES IT and SERVICES IT USES, AND WHO PAYS FOR THEM sit after the priced lines and BEFORE the exclusions, because a client reading 'what it covers' next asks who this is for and what else they must sign up for - answering those first means the exclusions read as the end of a complete picture rather than as the document's opening statement about its own limits. A client-paid service adds one standing sentence, once. A line says 'For: Customer' under its own features, and only when the quotation declared roles at all.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED by verify-quotation-scope, 41 checks (was 36): the three roles reach the row each with what they can do, the three third-party services reach it with whose bill each one is (two client-paid, one included, one carrying a charge the requirements established), three of the four lines carry the role they serve on their own item row, and each names the role its description implies in order. RED-PROVED THREE TIMES. Two unit: the referential check removed (2 of 29 go red) and one of the three item writes stripped of p_serves (1 goes red). One LIVE: the writer stopped from storing the parameter, pg_proc evidence printed either side, and the two audience checks go red - 41/41 restored after. THE LIVE RED-PROOF TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS AND THE FIRST TWO SILENTLY DID NOT RUN: `create function` was refused because the function already existed, then the mangled SQL broke the column list rather than the values list. Both were caught only because the evidence was printed before and after; a red-proof that reports zero failures because the control was never removed is the shape this repository has been caught by before.

gaps.title: what it costs to make: the owner's own pricing principle, and rates they can change
gaps.status: CLOSED - a quotation freezes what the work costs to produce and the owner's own multiplier bands above it, from rates the owner sets without a deploy
gaps.implementationState: TWO PRICING FINDINGS FROM ONE ZERO-TRUST AUDIT, closed together. FIRST: THERE WAS NO COST MODEL AT ALL. The owner's stated principle is production cost x2 / x2.5 / x3, and a search of the whole repository for a production cost, an AI cost, a margin, a markup or a multiplier returned nothing outside UI markup and per-run token accounting. So a quotation could sit BELOW what the work costs to build and nothing in the system would know - the one thing the corpus formula cannot see, because the corpus records what this agency CHARGED and not what it cost. SECOND: PRICING WAS CODE, NOT CONFIGURATION. pricing-reference.ts says so in its own docblock - 'If the agency's pricing moves, this file is WHERE it moves' - which is honest and means the owner cannot change their own pricing without an engineer and a deploy. Every input to the new model is an organization SETTING instead, written through core.set_organization_setting and audited exactly like the WhatsApp number and the contact block before it: a build day rate, an AI-and-tooling day rate, and the three multipliers. WHERE THE EFFORT COMES FROM: the model that wrote the line estimates its days, and that is the only honest source - the corpus timeline band is derived FROM the price, so using it here would make the cost a function of the price and the whole comparison circular. THREE REFUSALS KEEP IT HONEST, and all three are silence rather than an error. Unconfigured says nothing, so an agency that has set no rates behaves exactly as it did before this existed. Incoherent says nothing: a set where the minimum band exceeds the premium one produces three numbers in an order nobody can act on, and the honest answer to a contradiction is silence rather than a reading of it. Half-estimated says nothing: a cost built from three of five lines is an underestimate wearing a cost's clothes, and it would make the owner's floor look lower than it is, which is the direction that loses money. THE ORDER RULE IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THE DATABASE: set_organization_setting writes one key at a time and cannot see the other four, and an owner raising all three passes through an incoherent moment on the way. The reader refuses an out-of-order set, and the FORM refuses it at the point a person can fix it. WHAT IS CHECKED in the database is each value's own shape, for the reason the contact keys are: a rate typed '8,000' would parse to 8 and divide the agency's costs by a thousand, and a multiplier typed 250 would price at 250x cost. FROZEN AT DRAFT, like G-172's reference and for a sharper reason: these rates are now editable from a page, so a figure recomputed at render would judge an August quotation by today's costs. ADVISORY AND APPROVER-ONLY throughout: ADM-22 and ADM-07 leave the price with the owner, nothing blocks a draft, and none of it is ever drawn on a document a client receives. The note speaks only BELOW the owner's own minimum band, and says the harder thing plainly when the price is below cost itself - 'the agency pays to do it' is a different fact from 'under your target margin'.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED by verify-quotation-scope, 44 checks (was 41). The rates are set through the audited setter the owner's own form uses, the stub estimates 13 developer-days across four lines, and the quotation freezes 13 days at ₹1,30,000 with bands of ₹2,60,000 / ₹3,25,000 / ₹3,90,000 - against a draft asking ₹87,000, which is BELOW cost and is exactly the case this model exists to surface. The derivation is stored with the figure. The settings are cleared in the script's finally, and the demo tenant is left as it was found (verified empty after the run). The setter's own refusals were driven raw in psql first: '8000' set, '8,000' invalid_value, '2.5' set, '250' invalid_value, '1' invalid_value. RED-PROVED THREE TIMES: the half-estimated refusal removed (2 of 35 tests red), the five pricing keys stripped from the write GUARD while left in the setter (1 red - which is the shape that would let anybody with conversations_write set them unaudited), and LIVE, the freeze removed from the quotation.scope workflow (3 checks red, 44/44 restored).
gaps.testCoverage: tests/what-it-costs-to-make.test.ts (35): five settings make a model and any four make none; bands out of order make none; a multiplier at or below 1 is not a band; a day that costs nothing is an empty field that parsed, while AI costing nothing is a real answer; days x (build + AI) is the cost and the bands are the owner's multipliers; the derivation travels in the order it was applied; half-estimated, zero and NaN day counts are refused rather than extrapolated; no settings and an empty scope produce nothing. The note is silent at or above the minimum band, states the cost and the bands below it, says 'the agency pays to do it' below cost in different words from 'below your minimum band', names the decision as the owner's, and says nothing for a missing or corrupt block. The document round-trips the frozen block, a malformed one does not take the document with it, and the assembler is proved NOT to recompute. The schema takes a whole-day estimate and refuses a fraction; all three prompts ask for it, say it is all-or-nothing and say it never reaches the client; all three doors freeze it; and a failed settings read is proved unable to fail a draft. The migration: all five keys in the setter AND in the guard - the two lists are the same list twice - a comma-bearing rate refused, a percentage-shaped multiplier refused, the order deliberately absent from the database, and the form and the page carrying the rules the database cannot.

gaps.title: the owner's decision teaches the next quotation: nothing in this system learned anything
gaps.status: CLOSED - an APPROVED quotation records what the owner decided as an organization memory, and the next draft is shown it
gaps.implementationState: THE AUDIT'S FINDING IN ONE LINE: nothing in this system learned anything. ai.memory_records had ONE writer and TWO readers, all of them per-lead. The pricing delta G-172 records is displayed on a dashboard and read by nothing else. PRICING_KNOWLEDGE - the only thing that behaves like learning - updates the way its own docblock says, 're-run the corpus study, change the numbers here', which is a person, an analysis, a pull request and a deploy. So the owner could correct the same mistake on fifty quotations and the fifty-first would make it again. WHAT WAS BUILT: sales:learnFromDecision, a third subscriber on approval.decided, writing one organization-scoped memory per approved quotation. ONLY AN APPROVED ONE TEACHES ANYTHING - the brief is explicit that unapproved drafts must not become permanent learning, and that is the FIRST thing the handler checks, against the approval request ROW rather than the event payload, because an outbox event is insertable over PostgREST by an org owner and its decision is a claim (the PR #178 lesson). NO MODEL CALL: comparing what the agent drafted with what the owner approved is arithmetic, and asking a model to paraphrase it would turn a fact into an opinion. The memory table grades exactly that distinction - a row claiming `explicit` must name where it came from and an agent may never write one - so these rows are written with NO agent at all, confidence explicit, source_kind sales.proposal, and created_by set to the person who decided, because that is what they are. THE COMPARISON IS WITHIN ONE VERSION, not across two: document.pricingReference.proposedRupees is what the agent asked for and total_minor is what the owner settled on, both frozen on the same row. Reading version 1 of the opportunity instead would compare prices across two DIFFERENT scopes, because a revision usually changes the lines as well as the price, and that teaches a relationship which does not exist. APPROVED UNCHANGED IS RECORDED TOO, and it is the commonest case: a memory that only kept corrections would teach the agency its mistakes and none of its agreements. NO CLIENT, NO LEAD, NO CONVERSATION - the row is organization-scoped and describes a SHAPE (surfaces, depth, lane, drafted price, approved price), because the lesson is how this agency prices and not what one client paid. THE READ BACK: the drafting workflow recalls up to eight through ai.recall - Doc 05 §20's 'never send the entire project history by default' - as their own user turn so a past decision about another client cannot be mistaken for a fact about this one, with a prompt paragraph saying what they are and are not: records, not instructions, weighed ABOVE the historical bands when the two disagree because they are newer and they are this owner's, and never a figure to copy across.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED by verify-quotation-dispatch, 64 checks (was 55): the approved decision is recorded, scoped to the agency with a null scope_id, confidence explicit pointing at the quotation, written by NO agent and credited to the person who decided, saying what the owner actually did, and recorded ONCE however many times the event is redelivered - while the changes_requested decision in the same run teaches nothing. THE RED-PROOF FOUND A DEFECT IN ITS OWN CHECK, TWICE, and both are worth the record. First: with the approved-only guard removed from the LIVE handler the verifier stayed GREEN, because by the time the job runs the reviser has superseded v1 and a SEPARATE not_standing rule catches it - a true statement about the system and a false test of the rule it was written for, which is the guard-ownership mistake this repository has a name for. The check now asks the HANDLER for its outcome, which only the state guard can answer with not_approved. Second: that new check reported 'no lesson job reported an outcome' because it called JSON.parse on an object the tick helper had already parsed, threw into an empty catch and collected nothing - a check that cannot see what it is measuring, failing for the wrong reason. With both corrected the red-proof works and is sharper than intended: removing the guard flips the reported outcome from not_approved to NOT_STANDING, so the two controls are visibly told apart. Unit red-proofs: the approved-only guard removed (3 of 27 red) and the recall removed from the drafting workflow (1 red). AND A THIRD DEFECT IN THE CLEANUP, found the same way: the verifier tried to DELETE the memories it wrote and the database refused every time - 'a memory is superseded, never deleted (Doc 05 §32)' - so 36 rows accumulated across runs. That is not untidiness: a leftover pricing decision is recalled into the NEXT script's drafting prompt, which is the one place a stray fixture can change what a model writes. They are EXPIRED now, which ai.recall honours, and which keeps the history the table exists to keep. AND CI EXPOSED A FIXTURE COLLISION between verification scripts while this branch was in flight, which is fixed here. verify-approval-announcements inserted its own invoice and deliverable rungs WITHOUT clearing or checking them; approval_policies carries a partial unique index, so an insert made while another script's policy for the same subject is still live is REFUSED - silently, because nothing checked - and request_approval then resolves the LEFTOVER. When that leftover's audience is `client` it emits no approval.requested at all, so every announcement assertion in the script is about an event that was never going to exist. It passed on every developer machine, where the leftovers had long since been cleaned up, and failed on CI's fresh chain. PROVED by planting a client-audience invoice rung and running the script both ways: red without the fix, 55/55 green with it. The rungs are now cleared, planted and ASSERTED - a fixture nobody checks is a fixture that can be absent - and section 0c additionally asserts that the request under test was raised at all, so a no_policy answer reports itself in one line instead of as three misleading lines about announcements.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-owner-decision-teaches-the-next-quotation.test.ts (27): the sentence a decision becomes - a raise, a reduction that reads as one, approved-unchanged, and a pre-G-172 quotation with no reference that still produces a usable sentence and no empty brackets; only an approved quotation is recorded, and rejected, changes_requested and still-pending all write nothing; a superseded, draft, lapsed or rejected PROPOSAL writes nothing either while approved, sent and accepted do; an invoice decision is not a pricing lesson; one decision is recorded once; a failed read is retryable and a vanished request is not a failure at all; every refusal after the id check is a SUCCESS, because this handler owes nobody any state; it reads the frozen reference on the same version and never fetches another; it records the shape and never the client; the catalog routes the event to all three listeners in order, an invoice decision spends no job, the runner drains the queue and does it AFTER the dispatch because a client is waiting for that; and the drafting workflow recalls them organization-scoped, capped at eight, unable to fail a draft, as their own turn, with all three prompts saying what the records are and that a figure is never copied across. Two more pin the cleanup: the verifier expires rather than deletes, and ai.recall's own migration is what makes an expiry mean anything.

gaps.title: a group message can carry a file: a client's screenshot was counted as somebody else's traffic
gaps.status: CLOSED - a file posted into a group is recorded with its envelope, and a text message's metadata is byte-for-byte what it was
gaps.implementationState: FOUND BY READING THE WEBHOOK LINE BY LINE in a zero-trust audit: if (message.groupId && message.mediaType) { skipped += 1; continue; }. A photograph, a voice note or a PDF posted into a project group was counted as somebody else's traffic and thrown away. The comment beside it was honest about the trade - 'crm.ingest_group_message takes no media kind, and widening it is a separate change' - and named the loss it was accepting: an internal group losing a sticker is not the same as a client's voice note going unanswered on their lead thread. That was right about the PRIORITY and wrong about the OUTCOME. The project group IS the client-facing thread once a project starts (G-015, ADM-13), so the file a client posts there - the screenshot of the bug, the logo, the signed document - is exactly what an agency is later accused of never having received, and skipped made it indistinguishable from a message for a number nobody claims. WHAT IT DOES: stores the envelope the 1:1 path stores - media type, media id, caption - merged key by key so a TEXT message's metadata is byte-for-byte what it was before, with no null keys invented on it. WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO: queue a reading. image.received and audio.received exist so a client's file is understood before the agent ANSWERS it on a lead thread, and nothing answers a group thread automatically - crm.emit_reply_due fires on a client message in a DIRECT conversation and a group message is not that. A model call whose output nothing reads is cost with no consumer, the shape G-011 exists to refuse; the moment something does answer a group, this function is where the emit grows. The function is DROPPED and recreated rather than replaced - the overload trap G-178 hit one function along - and keeps every refusal it had: unknown_phone_number_id, unknown_group, replayed, the FOR UPDATE that serialises two participants posting at once, the on-conflict that makes a racing redelivery a replay, and the author-type rule that refuses to narrow a group to a person. ALSO CORRECTED HERE: the route's docblock said 'a reply is a later, human-gated step that does not exist yet', which stopped being true at ADM-91. The route was right the whole time; the comment was a trap for the next reader.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED by verify-group-ingest, 25 checks (was 19): a file posted into the group is recorded rather than dropped, with the type and the id the 1:1 path stores, with the words sent alongside it, still keyed to the group and still inbound - and a plain text message is still just a message, with no empty media keys invented on it. RED-PROVED TWICE, and the FIRST ATTEMPT WAS INVALID: the mangled SQL removed the comma between the metadata expression and p_occurred_at, so the function was BROKEN rather than control-free, and the evidence line still read 'stores media = true' because the parameter names survived. It reddened four checks for the wrong reason. Redone precisely - jsonb_build_object replaced by an empty object, evidence printed either side reading true then false - and then NARROWED to prove the checks discriminate rather than merely detect a crash: removing ONLY the caption reddens exactly one check, 'and the words they sent with it', and nothing else.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/a-group-message-can-carry-a-file.test.ts (9): the dropping branch is gone; the group path still routes a group message away from the lead-creating ingest, which is the only thing standing between the parser knowing about group_id and a colleague becoming a prospect; the stale docblock is replaced by what is actually true; the ingest passes the envelope through. The migration: dropped rather than overloaded, the new parameters appended with null defaults, every refusal and both locks still present, each metadata key merged only when it has a value, and no reading queued - with the reason stated where the next person will look.

gaps.title: the agent explains the quotation it sends: the client received a price list
gaps.status: CLOSED - the agent writes the words the client reads above the figures, approved with the price and unable to contain one
gaps.implementationState: A zero-trust audit walked the flow's CLIENT QUOTATION DELIVERY step and found nothing agent-shaped in it: the send composed a fixed template from the row - title, lines, total, validity - and nobody explained anything. A client who had spent a whole conversation being understood received a price list. TWO DECISIONS, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. (1) WRITTEN AT DRAFT TIME, NOT AT SEND TIME. The obvious place is the moment of sending and it is wrong twice over: a model call on the send path adds a failure mode to the one action a client is waiting for, and - far more importantly - words written AFTER the approval are words the owner never approved. The note rides in the approval announcement instead, quoted above the figures the way the client will read them, so the owner reads what the agent wrote before deciding. (2) IT MAY NOT CONTAIN A NUMBER. What makes agent-written client-facing prose about a PRICED quotation permissible under ADM-22 is not that it avoids figures, though it does - it is that the person who decides the price also decides what is said about it, and that is only true if they can see it. The figure rule is the second guard: quotationLanguageFault already refused a rupee amount in a quotation's prose, and the covering note joins the same prose LIST rather than getting a check of its own, so every rule about a quotation's language - open scope, unqualified readiness, amounts in prose - reaches it without being restated. A number written twice is a number that can disagree with itself, and the one in prose is the one no arithmetic gate checks. THE MIGRATION WAS REGENERATED FROM THE LIVE DEFINITION, and that is recorded because the first draft was not: written from memory, it silently lost the already_pending branch and the no-lines guard - the near miss PR #113 made and G-126 recorded, where a hand-rewritten function drops a branch and every structural test stays green. The shipped body is pg_get_functiondef output with exactly one line added, and a test asserts every outcome the function could answer before it still can. ALSO CORRECTED HERE, by measurement rather than assumption: the audit called the brief's '2-3+ page scope specification' PARTIAL, on the grounds that the schema caps made it impossible. Rendering a realistic quotation with everything G-177 and G-178 added produces THREE pages and 960 words, and the schema's maximum produces EIGHT pages and 1,775 words. The requirement is met, and raising the caps would only invite the padding the corpus study's own discipline forbids ('do not pad the plan to look thorough').
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED at both ends. verify-quotation-scope, 47 checks (was 44): the covering note the agent wrote reaches the row, carries no figure, AND rides in the approval payload - which is the line that makes the whole thing permissible, because the owner cannot approve words they never see. verify-quotation-dispatch, 66 checks (was 64): the message the client actually receives OPENS with the agent's note rather than with a price list, and every figure is still beneath it. RED-PROVED THREE TIMES, evidence printed either side of each. Unit: the note removed from the language guard's prose list (4 of 20 tests red - the guard that stops an agent writing a price into client-facing prose). Live: the payload stripped of covering_note (the owner-sees-it check goes red) and the composer stopped from putting the note on the wire - whose red output shows exactly the defect being fixed, a client message opening 'delivery app quotation - v1'.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/the-agent-explains-the-quotation.test.ts (20): a note is accepted; one carrying a rupee figure is refused, and so are Rs and INR, because the rule is about money and not one glyph; the fault names the note as its own location the way it names the summary and a line; an absent note breaks nothing that checked before it existed; and the open-scope rule reaches it too, because it joined the prose list rather than getting its own check. The client reads it first, with a blank line, and every figure is still printed beneath; without one the message is byte-for-byte what it was; both send doors read it from the same frozen document; the document round-trips it and a malformed one loses only it. The owner reads it before deciding: quoted, before the figures, and absent it announces exactly as it did. And the wiring: all three prompts ask for it and forbid a number, all three doors persist it, the payload carries it out of the document, and the function kept every refusal it had.

gaps.title: a price objection turns the loop: three of the four objections ended in a queue
gaps.status: CLOSED - a price objection against a quotation the client is holding redrafts and submits for the owner's decision; trust and timeline still never do
gaps.implementationState: A zero-trust audit traced the flow's NEGOTIATION step and found that three of the four objection kinds ended in a person's queue. Only a scope-change objection redrafted anything; a client saying 'that is too much for us' produced a row, a rank and nothing else. THE REASON GIVEN CONFLATED TWO THINGS. It was ADM-22's posture - the agent may not move a number under client pressure - but what ADM-22 forbids is a number reaching a CLIENT without a person deciding it, and A REWORK DECIDES NOTHING: it drafts a version and submits it for approval, exactly as the scope-change loop has since G-163, and the owner sees it before anybody else. Refusing to draft did not protect the price; it left the entire response to a person while the ask sat in a queue. THE OWNER DECIDED THIS on the audit, choosing the redraft loop explicitly. So the gate widened and the authority did not: the plan filter and the workflow's row-authority guard both take feature and price, and the reworked version still goes to the owner and never to the client. TRUST AND TIMELINE STILL NEVER ENTER IT - neither is a scope, and a client who does not trust you is not asking for a different quotation. THE CORPUS'S DISCIPLINE MOVED RATHER THAN WENT. 'Protect the number by cutting scope, never by discounting' now lives in the PROMPT, where it is an instruction about what to draft, instead of in the wiring, where it was an instruction not to draft at all. It is also sharper than before: return a SMALLER honest build - drop or defer the lines that cost the most and matter least, say plainly in the exclusions what is no longer there, and let the total fall because the work did. And the case the rule cannot answer is named rather than improvised: when they want everything for less, return the scope UNCHANGED at its original price, because a draft that quietly shaved the number would have made the owner's decision for them.
gaps.productionVerificationState: LIVE-PROVED by verify-quotation-dispatch, 69 checks (was 66). Section 7 was INVERTED - from 'no rework job is even planned' to 'a version is drafted AND the client was sent nothing', which is the property that actually matters and the one the old shape could not tell apart from doing nothing at all. TWO DEFECTS IN THE CHECK ITSELF, both found because it was made able to explain itself. First, it collected the agent's reasons in a SECOND loop after a tickUntil had already run the rework, so a failure said only 'no v3' - a check that consumes the thing it is about to measure cannot explain itself; merged into one loop it reported the agent's own words. Second, and only visible once it could: 'v2 is pending_approval; the client is not holding it'. The fixture was raising a price objection against a version the client had never seen, which the rework correctly refuses - the FIXTURE was wrong, not the code, and a check that could not explain itself would have been 'fixed' around that. Section 7 now plants its own client, gets a quotation approved and actually SENT, and then argues about the price, which is the only order in which a price objection means anything. RED-PROVED both ways at once: the plan filter reverted to feature-only turns 2 of 11 unit tests red and three live checks red, with the live one reporting 'nothing planned'.
gaps.testCoverage: tests/a-price-objection-turns-the-loop.test.ts (11): a price objection now plans a rework and a scope-change one still does; trust and timeline do not, and neither does any kind without a quotation named; the workflow's row-authority guard admits exactly the two kinds the plan filter plans, so a real objection cannot be dropped by one of them; the prompt states the rule as what to DO rather than as a refusal, says what 'smaller' means concretely, names the case the rule cannot answer, and no longer carries the sentence saying a price push is not the agent's business - a prompt that contradicts the wiring is worse than one that says nothing. Read with codeOnly for claims about code and RAW for claims about prose, because the reasoning a change rests on is worth pinning too and lives in comments by definition.

adminDecisions.title: Verifying a WhatsApp number: ask Meta, or gate the setting behind a review?
adminDecisions.why: An owner can set their organization's whatsapp_phone_number_id to a number they do not own. Since D22's unique index the effect is no longer a silent capture - it is a denial of configuration, because the rightful agency's write is then refused with a bare 409. Two shapes: verify ownership against the Graph API at configuration time, which needs a token with permission to ask and must decide what to do when Meta is unreachable; or leave the field free and gate it behind an operator review, which needs somebody to do the reviewing. Neither is obviously right, and the current behaviour - first writer wins, permanently - is the one nobody chose. This row said an Admin decision was required and named none, which is G-107. || OWNER DECISION 2026-08-14 - GRANTED, option B: provider OAuth / Embedded Signup identity binding. Owner's stated reason: AgencyOS must not treat a manually typed WhatsApp number as sufficient proof of ownership; the number must be associated with AgencyOS through the provider's authenticated business identity. TEN IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS, recorded as given: (1) do not implement ownership based solely on a typed phone number; (2) do not assume an Admin-entered phone_number_id is proof of ownership; (3) bind the integration to the authenticated provider/business identity returned by the provider flow; (4) store the provider identifiers required to establish the binding; (5) enforce tenant isolation at the database/application boundary; (6) prevent the same number being claimed by two organizations; (7) preserve an auditable record of who connected the integration, which organization, provider/business identifiers, connection time and verification/connection status; (8) do not store provider secrets in the database unless the architecture explicitly requires encrypted secret storage; (9) production credentials remain in the platform secret store; (10) no AI agent may independently establish or change WhatsApp ownership. EXTERNAL VERIFICATION REQUIRED before implementation: provider eligibility, permissions, business verification and the exact current Embedded Signup integration flow are all UNKNOWN and are not to be invented. SEPARATE REQUIREMENT APPROVED: an operator/admin release path for an incorrectly claimed or disconnected number, which must not let arbitrary users detach another organization's integration. Raised as its own gap rather than implemented.
